docs.title: 11.3. Installation and Execution
docs.text: The application is located in the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder, next to the [exemples] folder. It is a standalone project, with its own [composer.json] and [.env] files, and its own [vendor] folder. The [README.md] file in the folder contains all of the following. The introduction to this document has already described the installation of [PHP] and [Composer]; we’ll expand on that here.

docs.title: 11.3.1. Required Software
docs.text:
Three software programs are all you need:

  • [PHP] 8.4 or later, with the extensions [pdo_mysql] and [intl] ([Symfony] 8 requires [PHP] 8.4, and the application uses features introduced in that version, such as [array_find]). Verify the installation in a terminal:
php -v
php -m

The second command lists the extensions: [pdo_mysql] and [intl] should be listed there;

  • [Composer], the library manager for [PHP] (see appendices);
  • a [MySQL] 8 server, for example, the one for [Laragon] under [Windows] (see appendices). [MariaDB] is also suitable.

The recommended editor is [Visual Studio Code], with the extensions [PHP Intelephense] and [Twig Language 2] (see appendices); however, everything can be done via the command line.

docs.title: 11.3.2. Install the libraries
docs.text:
The [vendor] folder is not provided: create it once and for all in a terminal window opened in the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder (you must be connected to the Internet):

composer install

[Composer] reads the file [composer.json] (discussed later), downloads [Symfony], [Doctrine], [Twig], [firebase/php-jwt], and the libraries they depend on, and generates the class loader [vendor/autoload.php], as well as the file [vendor/autoload_runtime.php] for the component [Runtime] (discussed below).

docs.title: 11.3.3. Create the database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database is created by the [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. Using [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu. At the command line, in the application folder:

mysql -u root -p < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql

The [-p] option prompts for the password for [root]; omit it if the account does not have a password (as is the case with [Laragon]). This is the same database as in other versions of the application: if it already exists, this step is optional. The script can be run at any time to revert to the original data.

docs.title: 11.3.4. Configure Database Access
docs.text: All installation configuration is contained in the file [.env] (discussed below). By default, the application connects to [MySQL] on [127.0.0.1], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password: these are the default settings for [Laragon]. If your [root] account has a password, enter it in this file, in the URL [DATABASE_URL] line, after [root:]. A system environment variable takes precedence over the file (example 25): this allows you to specify the database’s URL without writing it to a project file.

docs.title: 11.3.5. Launch the application
docs.text:
In a terminal window open to the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder:

php -S localhost:8081 -t public

[Sun Sep 27 18:40:12 2026] PHP 8.4.21 Development Server (http://localhost:8081) started

Next, open the URL [http://localhost:8081] in a browser, and stop the application using [Ctrl-C]. Port 8081 allows you to run a sample from the course (port 8000) at the same time. The command-line tool [symfony] (see appendices) provides a more comprehensive server that can also serve the application in HTTPS: [symfony server:start --port=8081].

docs.title: 11.3.6. Demo Accounts
docs.text:
The password for each account is its username; you must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase:

[admin]ADMIN (the administrator)[pelissier], [tatou], [dupont]DOCTOR (the doctors)[martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german]USER (patients)

A guide to exploring the app:

  • [admin]: Calendar, Ms. Marie PELISSIER; today: a time slot is already booked by Ms. Brigitte BISTROU. Book a slot for Mr. Jean MARTIN, then try to book a second appointment for him (declined). Doctors and Clients menus: add, edit, delete (Dr. PELISSIER, who has appointments, cannot be deleted);
  • [pelissier]: his daily schedule is displayed directly; the address [/medecins], entered manually, returns a 403 error page;
  • [martin]: My Account, their appointment, the calendar where other patients appear as “Reserved”; Manage My Account;
  • login page: Create a customer account, then log in with the new account;
  • Buttons FR / EN: The entire interface changes languages, including dates.

docs.title: 11.3.7. Development Mode
docs.text:
The provided file [.env] configures the application for development ([APP_ENV=dev]):

  • The server console displays the log for [Symfony] (example 24): the selected route, security steps, and each SQL command sent to the database (example 28). For example, to display a calendar (abbreviated lines):
[info] Matched route "agenda".
[debug] Checking for authenticator support.
[debug] Checking support on authenticator.
[info] Authenticator successful!
[debug] Authenticator set no success response: request continues.
[info] Connecting with parameters [array]
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT m0_.id AS id_0, ..., u1_.login AS login_7, ... FROM medecins m0_ INNER JOIN users u1_ ON m0_.`user` = u1_.`id` WHERE m0_.id = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT r0_.id AS id_0, ... FROM rv r0_ INNER JOIN clients c1_ ON r0_.id_client = c1_.id INNER JOIN creneaux c2_ ON r0_.id_creneau = c2_.id WHERE r0_.jour = ? AND c2_.id_medecin = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT c0_.id AS id_0, ... FROM creneaux c0_ WHERE c0_.id_medecin = ? ORDER BY c0_.hdebut ASC, c0_.mdebut ASC (parameters: [array], types: [array])
127.0.0.1:55220 [200]: GET /agenda?idMedecin=1&jour=2026-09-27
[info] Disconnecting

Here we can see the routing, the authenticator, and then three requests: the doctor and their account, today’s appointments and their patients, and the doctor’s available time slots. The list of doctors in the drop-down menu, however, is not read; it comes from the cache (discussed later);

  • an unexpected exception displays the [Symfony] debug page (example 03), with the exception message and the call stack. In production, the application displays its own 500 error page instead;
  • there is nothing to restart after a change: each request re-reads the [PHP] files (example 01), and, in [dev] mode, [Symfony] rebuilds its own cache (the container, routes, and compiled views) when a file has changed.

The [Xdebug] debugger also allows you to step through the application from [Visual Studio Code] ([PHP Debug] extension): This is an extension of [PHP], which must be installed separately (see xdebug.org). The debug bar in [Symfony] ([WebProfilerBundle], [composer require --dev symfony/web-profiler-bundle]) displays the query details at the bottom of each page: the route, the user, the SQL commands and their parameters, translations, execution times...

docs.title: 11.3.8. A production server
docs.text:
The [PHP] development server is not intended for production. In production, the application is served by a web server ([nginx], [Apache]), which forwards requests to [PHP-FPM], a process manager ([PHP]). The site root is the [public] folder: only its files are accessible from the browser; the [var] folder must be writable by the server. In the [.env] file, you must specify production mode, change the secret keys, and declare that the site is served from HTTPS:

APP_ENV=prod
APP_SECRET=<une longue chaîne aléatoire>
JWT_SECRET=<une autre longue chaîne aléatoire>
COOKIE_SECURE=1

A suitable random string can be obtained from [PHP] itself: [php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32));"]. The application is then prepared using two commands:

composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
php bin/console cache:clear

The second command generates the production cache (the compiled container, routes, compiled views, etc.): in [prod] mode, [Symfony] no longer checks whether the files have changed, which is faster; therefore, it must be rerun after every modification. The [composer dump-env prod] command also converts the [.env] file into a [PHP] ([.env.local.php]) file, which is read more quickly.

docs.title: 11.3.9. Common Issues
docs.text:
A [PHP] application does not “start”: each request rebuilds the application (example 01). An inaccessible database therefore does not prevent the server from starting: the error appears on the first page that queries the database (the login page does not query the database; the connection process does). In [dev] mode, the error is displayed on the [Symfony] debug page; in all cases, it is logged in the log file, which the development server displays in the console. For example, with a database that does not exist:

[critical] Uncaught PHP Exception Doctrine\DBAL\Exception\ConnectionException: "An exception occurred in the driver: SQLSTATE[HY000] [1049] Unknown database 'dbinconnue'" at ExceptionConverter.php line 91

The most common messages:

[Failed opening required '.../vendor/autoload_runtime.php']The command [composer install] was not executed[Your Composer dependencies require a PHP version ">= 8.4.0"]The version of [PHP] is older than 8.4[could not find driver]The extension [pdo_mysql] for [PHP] is not enabled (file [php.ini], or menu PHP / Extensions menu in [Laragon])[SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] Connection refused][MySQL] has not started, or is not listening on [127.0.0.1:3306][SQLSTATE[HY000] [1045] Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost']The password for [MySQL] must be entered in [DATABASE_URL] (see “Configuring Database Access”)[SQLSTATE[HY000] [1049] Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2']The script [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] was not executed[JWT_SECRET doit comporter au moins 32 caractères (cf. .env).]The secret key for the tokens is too short in [.env][Failed to listen on localhost:8081 (reason: Address already in use)]Port 8081 is already in use (is another version of the application running?): stop it, or choose a different port

docs.title: 11.4. Application Architecture
docs.text:
• The browser sends its requests to the server ([php -S], or [nginx] + [PHP-FPM]), which forwards them to [Symfony] via the file [public/index.php]. The core of [Symfony] publishes events related to request processing (see the chapter on the lifecycle), to which listeners respond: the request language ([FixerLangue]), routing, the session, and then the security component’s firewall: The user is identified based on the JWT token from their cookie ([JetonAuthenticator]), and the [access_control] rules deny access to protected pages for visitors who are not authorized. Errors result in pages HTML ([PageErreur]);
  • [Controller]: the web layer controllers. They all pass through a single object, [ApplicationModel] (folder [Web]), which caches the lists of doctors and clients and forwards other requests to the business layer; [Form]: forms and their constraints; [Vues]: view templates;
  • [Securite]: tokens, JWT, the authenticator, the CAPTCHA, the attempt limit, and the account creation pass;
  • [Web]: What controllers have in common: the cache and the facade [ApplicationModel], the parent class of controllers, flash messages, and a few utilities;
  • [Metier]: business rules and transactions;
  • [Dao]: the DAO layer, one class per table;
  • [Entity]: the entities [Doctrine], which the DAO layer reads from and writes to the database; [Domain]: the calendar objects, calculated by the business layer;
  • [templates]: the [Twig] views, which generate the HTML pages; [translations]: the dictionaries; [public]: the stylesheet, the page script, and [Bootstrap];
  • the [config] folder and the [.env] file: the configuration, which brings everything together.

[Bootstrap] is part of the application (folder [public/lib/bootstrap]) this time: the case study is self-contained.

docs.title: 11.5. The database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database has five tables:

  • [users]: users authorized to log in;
  • [medecins] and [clients]: doctors and patients, each linked to their user account;
  • [creneaux]: each doctor’s available time slots;
  • [rv]: appointments, one client per time slot on a given day.

docs.title: 11.5.1. database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
-- Database [dbrdvmedecins2] - MySQL 8
--
-- Changes to [dbrdvmedecins]:
--    1. The tables [medecins] and [clients] are added with a column named [user],
--       foreign key to users(id): every doctor and every client is
--       now also a user capable of logging in;
--    2. A third role appears: DOCTOR (in addition to ADMIN and USER);
--    3. The script creates a row [users] for each doctor (role DOCTOR)
--       and for each client (role USER):
--         -        login = name in lowercase
--         - password = name in lowercase, hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds)
--         - displ ay name = first name + last name
--
--    4. uniqueness constraints, all NOMMÉES (the application recognizes
--       the name of the violated constraint in the error message MySQL):
--         - unq_users         _login : a login belongs to only one account;
--         - unq_medecins_pren om_nom : Two doctors cannot have the
--                                      same first and last names;
--         - unq_clients_pren  om_nom : the same applies to clients.
--       Note: the utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation compares without taking into account
--       no capital letters or accents—"Hélène DUPONT" and "helene dupont"
--       are therefore considered identical.
--
-- The table [users] must now be created AVANT [medecins] and [clients]
-- (they reference it), and delete APRÈS them.
-- =========================================================================

-- The script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;

-- we start with an empty database each time the script runs (useful during development)
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins2 CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins2;

-- Deletion order: from “child” tables to “parent” tables
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rv;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS creneaux;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS medecins;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: users authorized to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- login ID
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- HACHÉ password (bcrypt) — never stored in plain text
  nom      VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- display name after login
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- 'ADMIN', 'DOCTOR', or 'USER'
   -- A login can only be associated with a single account
  CONSTRAINT unq_users_login UNIQUE (login)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [medecins]: the practice’s doctors
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE medecins (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,      -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,               -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,                 -- Ms., Mrs., Mr.
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`  INT NOT NULL,                         -- Foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_medecins_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
   -- one account per doctor, and one doctor per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_medecins_user UNIQUE (`user`),
   -- No two doctors can have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_medecins_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: doctors' patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`  INT NOT NULL,                         -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_clients_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
   -- One account per customer, and one customer per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_user UNIQUE (`user`),
   -- Two clients cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [creneaux]: each doctor’s appointment slots
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE creneaux (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  id_medecin INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  hdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start time of the time slot
  mdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start minute of the time slot
  hfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- slot end hour
  mfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- end minute of the time slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_creneaux_medecin FOREIGN KEY (id_medecin) REFERENCES medecins(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [rv]: appointments made by customers
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE rv (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  jour       DATE NOT NULL,                      -- appointment date
  id_creneau INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> time slots (id)
  id_client  INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> customers(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_creneau FOREIGN KEY (id_creneau) REFERENCES creneaux(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_client  FOREIGN KEY (id_client)  REFERENCES clients(id),
   -- The same time slot on the same day can only be booked once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE (jour, id_creneau)
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

-- Users: Passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds of salting)
--    admin/admin (ADMIN)
--    One account (DOCTOR) per doctor, one account (USER) per client
--    (the demo account user/user has been removed: a USER account is
--    is now TOUJOURS, a client account that allows the client to make reservations and manage their account)
--    (username = password = name in lowercase)
INSERT INTO users (login, password, nom, role) VALUES
  ('admin',     '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrateur',   'ADMIN'),
   -- doctors
  ('pelissier', '$2b$10$DnSDOK5ONrdMxTTr1NKCHOphR3WSp5QAyG9S9ueruw9HwlxI.16ba', 'Marie PELISSIER',  'DOCTOR'),
  ('tatou',     '$2b$10$PeovBO.gmJUKP4PglI/fwu4xtWOYSxoM5VTWjTj7uQ4wcd9P9.htS', 'Paul TATOU',       'DOCTOR'),
  ('dupont',    '$2b$10$az7wvPKC1h0EiAxXwu/PU.vYjzmB04rd5B7QnK0mvxp4niYIHVoc.', 'Sophie DUPONT',    'DOCTOR'),
   -- clients
  ('martin',    '$2b$10$GT6S5pp.WdGapFw/UmocXesbC6LEjJfZzgatCUyG9Sf4o1iBNlqZW', 'Jean MARTIN',      'USER'),
  ('durand',    '$2b$10$l2gl/zCder8E7Nh4VxGRX.0.SsO3FDiXt6YwqYq3v9nFzgC/jQCy6', 'Alice DURAND',     'USER'),
  ('bistrou',   '$2b$10$naeRp2YUU6c.QDl5itJMAum3Y5aHdUV6jwIcsbp0D.64jPG4F6E9m', 'Brigitte BISTROU', 'USER'),
  ('german',    '$2b$10$tTWxh3ROWF7NjhZOMnWDMOsZcnSWUiwwfy5C3G0.xhccTXALKyLeW', 'Luc GERMAN',       'USER');

-- doctors: the column [user] is retrieved based on the login,
-- rather than assuming the primary key values of [users]
INSERT INTO medecins (titre, nom, prenom, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mme',  'PELISSIER', 'Marie',  (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'pelissier')),
  ('Mr',   'TATOU',     'Paul',   (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'tatou')),
  ('Melle','DUPONT',    'Sophie', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'dupont'));

INSERT INTO clients (titre, nom, prenom, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mr',   'MARTIN',  'Jean',     (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'martin')),
  ('Mme',  'DURAND',  'Alice',    (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'durand')),
  ('Melle','BISTROU', 'Brigitte', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'bistrou')),
  ('Mr',   'GERMAN',  'Luc',      (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'german'));

-- Dr. PELISSIER’s time slots (id_medecin = 1): from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. in 20-minute increments
INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
  (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), (1, 8, 40, 9, 0),
  (1, 9, 0, 9, 20), (1, 9, 20, 9, 40), (1, 9, 40, 10, 0),
  (1, 10, 0, 10, 20), (1, 10, 20, 10, 40), (1, 10, 40, 11, 0),
  (1, 11, 0, 11, 20), (1, 11, 20, 11, 40), (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

-- Dr. TATOU’s time slots (id_medecin = 2): 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM in 20-minute increments
INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
  (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), (2, 14, 40, 15, 0),
  (2, 15, 0, 15, 20), (2, 15, 20, 15, 40), (2, 15, 40, 16, 0),
  (2, 16, 0, 16, 20), (2, 16, 20, 16, 40), (2, 16, 40, 17, 0),
  (2, 17, 0, 17, 20), (2, 17, 20, 17, 40), (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

-- an appointment already scheduled, to immediately see a slot that is occupied in the calendar
INSERT INTO rv (jour, id_creneau, id_client) VALUES
  (CURDATE(), 2, 3);
  • line 33: the database is created if it does not exist, with the character set [utf8mb4] and the collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci], which compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents (example 28);
  • lines 37–41: the tables are dropped and then recreated; the script restores the database to its initial state. The order matters: a table cannot be dropped as long as another table references it via a foreign key;
  • Lines 46–55: Users: a username and a password hashed with [bcrypt] (example 25), the display name after logging in, and the role ([ADMIN], [DOCTOR], or [USER]). The constraint [unq_users_login] ensures that a username belongs to only one account;
  • Lines 60–72: Each table has a primary key [id], generated by the database, and a column [version], which is the optimistic lock (Example 28). The column [user] is a foreign key referencing [users(id)]: the database rejects any value that is not the ID of an existing user. Since [user] is a word in the SQL language, it is surrounded by grave accents. Three constraints: [fk_medecins_user] (the foreign key), [unq_medecins_user] (one account per doctor, and one doctor per account), and [unq_medecins_prenom_nom] (no homonyms). All constraints are named: the application recognizes a violated constraint by its name;
  • lines 77–89: the customer table has exactly the same columns;
  • lines 94–103: a time slot belongs to a doctor; its start and end times are stored in hours and minutes;
  • lines 108–118: an appointment consists of a day (type [DATE], without a time), a time slot, and a client. The constraint [unq1_rv] prevents the same time slot from being booked twice on the same day: the database enforces this rule, even if two users attempt to book it at the same time;
  • lines 130–140: demo users, whose password is their login. The hashes begin with [$2b$10$]: the algorithm ([bcrypt], variant [2b]) and the cost (10). Next come the salt and the hash. These hashes were calculated by the [Flask] version of the application; [PHP] writes its own with the prefix [$2y$], but verifies both equally well;
  • lines 144–147: the [user] column for each doctor is retrieved via a subquery based on the login, rather than by assuming the values of the primary keys;
  • lines 170–171: an appointment already scheduled for today ([CURDATE()]) in Dr. PELISSIER’s second time slot for Ms. BISTROU: the calendar thus immediately shows a booked time slot.

Unlike in the case of [Symfony], the database is not created by [Doctrine] from the entities, nor through migrations (example 28): it is shared with the other versions of the application, and the script SQL is common to all of them. The command [php bin/console doctrine:schema:validate] verifies that the entity descriptions are consistent and that they correspond to the database tables.

docs.title: 11.6.1. composer.json
docs.text:
{
    "name": "rdvmedecins/rdvmedecins2-symfony",
    "description": "RdvMedecins : prise de rendez-vous médicaux, pages HTML fabriquées par le serveur (Symfony + Twig + Doctrine)",
    "type": "project",
    "license": "MIT",
    "require": {
        "php": ">=8.4",
        "ext-intl": "*",
        "ext-pdo_mysql": "*",
        "doctrine/doctrine-bundle": "^3.3",
        "doctrine/orm": "^3.7",
        "firebase/php-jwt": "^7.2",
        "symfony/asset": "^8.1",
        "symfony/console": "^8.1",
        "symfony/dotenv": "^8.1",
        "symfony/form": "^8.1",
        "symfony/framework-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/lock": "^8.1",
        "symfony/rate-limiter": "^8.1",
        "symfony/runtime": "^8.1",
        "symfony/security-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/translation": "^8.1",
        "symfony/twig-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/validator": "^8.1",
        "symfony/yaml": "^8.1",
        "twig/twig": "^3.30"
    },
    "autoload": {
        "psr-4": {
            "App\\": "src/"
        }
    },
    "config": {
        "allow-plugins": {
            "symfony/runtime": true
        },
        "optimize-autoloader": true,
        "sort-packages": true
    },
    "minimum-stability": "stable",
    "prefer-stable": true
}
  • Lines 6–27: the libraries required by the application and the constraints they must meet. [^8.1] reads “version 8.1 or a newer version of the same major version 8”: [Composer] accepts versions that fix bugs or add features, but not those that could break the application (version 9). The lines [php], [ext-intl], and [ext-pdo_mysql] do not refer to libraries, but to environment requirements: [Composer] will refuse installation if the version of [PHP] or its extensions are incompatible, rather than allowing the application to fail later. [Symfony] is not a single library: each of its components (routing, forms, security, etc.) is a library, and the application requests only those it needs; [Composer] additionally installs the libraries on which they depend;
  • Lines 28–32: The application’s PSR-4 rule: classes in the [App] namespace are located in the [src] folder (Example 01: In the examples, the file [public/index.php] itself declared this rule to the class loader via [addPsr4]);
  • Lines 34–36: The component [Runtime] is a plugin (plugin) for [Composer]; it runs during installation to write the file [vendor/autoload_runtime.php]. [Composer] requests permission to execute a plugin’s code; this permission is granted here.

[composer install] installs the versions that meet these constraints and records the exact versions installed in a file named [composer.lock]. Subsequent installations (on another machine, for example) use this file: they install exactly the same versions. [composer update], on the other hand, searches for the most recent versions permitted by [composer.json] and updates [composer.lock]. The command [composer show] lists what is installed in the [vendor] folder. In a typical project, this file is supplemented by [Symfony Flex] for each [composer require] (example 01).

docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# .env: settings specific to the CETTE installation, read at the start of each
# request by the Dotenv component (see public/index.php). They become
# environment variables, which the configuration (config folder) reads via
# %env(NOM)%. A genuine system environment variable takes precedence over this file.
# =========================================================================

# dev: development; prod: production (see README.md)
APP_ENV=dev
# the Symfony secret key (anti-CSRF tokens, signatures, etc.). In production:
# another value, long and random
APP_SECRET=34b2364cc4c93df6e4ee35251a048088

# ---- the database MySQL [dbrdvmedecins2] (script: database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql):
# SGBD, the username and password (for Laragon: root, no password
# password), the server, its port, the database, and the server version (for MariaDB:
# serverVersion=10.11.2-MariaDB, for example) and the character set
DATABASE_URL="mysql://root:@127.0.0.1:3306/dbrdvmedecins2?serverVersion=8.0.32&charset=utf8mb4"

# ---- authentication (see src/Securite/AuthService.php)
# secret key for tokens JWT: at least 32 characters (HMAC-SHA256)
JWT_SECRET=ef1cfc9709f10b5b5d183b4deb6d5dbbe69518629c3b12a8
# token validity period, in minutes (120 min = 2 h)
JWT_DUREE_MINUTES=120
# 1 in production (site served as HTTPS): cookies are never transmitted in plain text
COOKIE_SECURE=0

# ---- protection against bots (see src/Securite/LimiteurTentatives.php)
# allowed login failures for the same login from the same address IP, then
# blocking for this duration (in minutes); an address IP is also blocked if it
# accumulates LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP failed login attempts across all logins (a bot attempting
# thousands of different logins)
LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS=5
LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP=25
LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES=15
# customer accounts created per hour and per IP address. In the classroom, all
# Items are often shipped from the same address: increase if necessary
INSCRIPTION_MAX_PAR_HEURE=10

The file containing settings specific to this installation (example 25): these vary from one machine to another (the database, its credentials) or are confidential (the keys). In a real project, production secrets are not included here: they are provided by actual environment variables, by a [.env.local] file that is never published, or by the [Symfony] secrets vault (example 25).

  • line 9: the application mode: [dev] (development: debug mode, debug page, cache rebuilt with every change) or [prod];
  • line 12: the secret key for [Symfony], which is used in particular for anti-CSRF tokens (example 21);
  • line 18: the database connection (example 28);
  • lines 20–38: application-specific settings: the JWT tokens (example 25) and bot protection (example 27).

docs.title: 11.6.3. config/bundles.php and config/packages/framework.yaml
docs.text:
<?php
// config/bundles.php: the application's bundles (see example 01): the core of
// Symfony, Twig views, security, and Doctrine (database access)
return [
    Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\FrameworkBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Symfony\Bundle\TwigBundle\TwigBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Symfony\Bundle\SecurityBundle\SecurityBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Doctrine\Bundle\DoctrineBundle\DoctrineBundle::class => ['all' => true],
];

The application’s four bundles: the core [Symfony], [Twig] (Example 13), security (Example 25), and [Doctrine] (Example 28).

# =========================================================================
# config/packages/framework.yaml: FrameworkBundle configuration
# =========================================================================
framework:
    secret: '%env(APP_SECRET)%'

     # ---- Languages (see Example 22): French (default), English; the
     # translation service and its dictionaries (translations folder)
    default_locale: fr
    enabled_locales: ['fr', 'en']
    translator:
        default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/translations'
        fallbacks: ['fr']

     # ---- form validation: its messages are CLÉS from our
     # dictionaries (ERRORS.FIRSTNAME_REQUIRED...), translated in the
     # [messages], the same as that of the views (default: the [validators] domain)
    validation:
        translation_domain: messages

     # ---- SESSION (flash messages, anti-CSRF tokens): files in the
     # var/sessions. The session cookie is never readable by the JavaScript from
     # the page (httponly), nor is it sent with a request from another site
     # (samesite lax), nor, in production, sent in plain text (secure)
    session:
        handler_id: null
        save_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/var/sessions/%kernel.environment%'
        name: rdvmedecins_session
        cookie_httponly: true
        cookie_samesite: lax
        cookie_secure: '%env(bool:COOKIE_SECURE)%'
    csrf_protection: true

     # ---- the locks (see example 20), for the attempt limiters
    lock: 'flock://%kernel.project_dir%/var/lock'

     # ---- attempt locks (see example 27 and src/Securite/LIMITEURS).
     # fixed_window: a maximum of [limit] attempts per [interval] period, counted
     # starting with the first attempt
    rate_limiter:
         # connection failures for a login, from an address IP
        login:
            policy: fixed_window
            limit: '%env(int:LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS)%'
            interval: '%env(LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES)% minutes'
         # login failures for an address IP, across all logins
        login_ip:
            policy: fixed_window
            limit: '%env(int:LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP)%'
            interval: '%env(LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES)% minutes'
         # accounts created from an address IP, by hour
        inscription:
            policy: fixed_window
            limit: '%env(int:INSCRIPTION_MAX_PAR_HEURE)%'
            interval: '1 hour'
  • lines 9–13: languages and the translator (Example 22);
  • lines 18–19: the validation component translates its messages into the [validators] domain (example 09); Our constraints use keys from our dictionaries ([ERRORS.FIRSTNAME_REQUIRED]...) as message keys, which are in the [messages] domain: we specify this to the validation component. Thus, a single dictionary per language is sufficient for the entire application;
  • Lines 25–32: the session (example 20): files in the [var/sessions] folder. The application stores very little there: flash messages and anti-CSRF tokens. The session cookie is named [rdvmedecins_session]; it is never readable by the [JavaScript] on the page, nor is it sent with a POST request from another site, nor, in production, sent in plain text (the prefix [bool:] converts the variable to a Boolean, example 25);
  • line 35: the locks (example 20), used by the attempt limiters and the CAPTCHA service;
  • lines 40–55: the three anti-bot limiters (example 27), whose settings come from the file [.env]. A value may combine text and a variable: ['15 minutes'].

The application cache (the [cache.app] service, Example 20) does not need to be configured: it is stored in files within the [var/cache/dev/pools] (or [prod]) folder. The application stores lists of doctors and clients, CAPTCHAs, attempt counters, and passes there—all of which must be shared across all requests. With multiple servers, you would choose a shared cache, such as [Redis] ([framework.cache.app: cache.adapter.redis]).

docs.title: 11.6.4. config/packages/security.yaml
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# config/packages/security.yaml: security (see examples 25 and 26)
# =========================================================================
security:
     # account password hashes: bcrypt, 10 rounds, like the
     # hashes from the SQL script. PHP also verifies the $2b$ (Python) and $2a$
     # (Java) hashes from other versions of the application, which share the same database
    password_hashers:
        App\Entity\User:
            algorithm: bcrypt
            cost: 10

     # the user provider: not applicable here; the logged-in user is
     # identified by their token (see src/Securite/JetonAuthenticator.php); Symfony, however,
     # requires, however, an empty list
    providers:
        aucun:
            memory: ~

    firewalls:
         # UN firewall for the entire application, SANS ÉTAT: the user is not
         # stored in the session; the user is identified for each request using the token
         # JWT from their cookie
        principal:
            stateless: true
            provider: aucun
            custom_authenticators:
                - App\Securite\JetonAuthenticator

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
     # LA RÈGLE D'ACCÈS: The rules are examined in order; the first one whose
     # whose path matches the path of URL applies:
        # - some URL PUBLIQUES (PUBLIC_ACCESS): the home page, login,
          # language selection, account creation;
        # - URL reserved for certain roles (a list of roles: UN of them is sufficient);
        # - all AUTRES require an authenticated user (last rule).
     # This is the “everything is prohibited unless explicitly permitted” rule: a URL added
     # later, and if we had forgotten to protect it, it is automatically protected.
     # A denied anonymous visitor is redirected to the login page (the
     # firewall entry point); an authenticated user without the requested role
     # receives a 403 error page.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    access_control:
        - { path: ^/$, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
        - { path: ^/(login|logout)$, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
        - { path: ^/langue/, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
        - { path: ^/inscription, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
         # A patient cancels SON an appointment from “My Account,” not from the calendar
        - { path: ^/agenda/annuler$, roles: [ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_DOCTOR] }
        - { path: ^/(medecins|clients), roles: ROLE_ADMIN }
        - { path: ^/mon-, roles: ROLE_USER }
        - { path: ^/, roles: IS_AUTHENTICATED }

Security configuration (examples 25 and 26):

  • Lines 8–11: Password hashing: [bcrypt], 10 rounds, like the hashes in the script SQL. To verify a password, [PHP] reads the algorithm and cost from the hash itself: the hashes in the database, written by [Python] ([$2b$]) or by [Java] ([$2a$]), are verified just as much as those of [PHP] ([$2y$]);
  • lines 16–18: the user provider. The application authenticator does not need one: the logged-in user is identified by their token, without reading the database (example 25). But the security component requires one: a provider [memory], with no users;
  • lines 24–28: a single, stateless firewall for the entire application, with our authenticator. No pattern ([pattern]): it covers all URL. The files in the [public] folder ([Bootstrap], the stylesheet, the script) do not pass through [Symfony]: the web server serves them directly;
  • Lines 43–52: the application’s access rule. The [access_control] rules are evaluated in order, and the first one whose pattern matches the path of URL is applied. [PUBLIC_ACCESS] grants access to URL to everyone, including anonymous visitors: the home page, login, language selection, and account creation. Next come the URL rules reserved for certain roles: a list of roles (line 49) means that any one of them is sufficient. The last rule, [^/], applies to all remaining URL rules and requires an authenticated user. This is the “everything is prohibited except what is permitted” rule: a URL added later—even if you forgot to protect it—is automatically protected. The opposite error—a public URL that was accidentally left unprotected—is immediately apparent; the error of a forgotten protected page is much less so.

Roles are verified here, in a single file, using URL patterns, rather than [#[IsGranted]] attributes on actions (example 26): both are possible and can be combined.

docs.title: 11.7.1. public/index.php and bin/console
docs.text:
<?php
// public/index.php: the entry point for TOUTES requests. The folder
// [public] is the site root: only its files are accessible from the
// browser (Bootstrap, stylesheet, script)—never the application code.
//
// The file vendor/autoload_runtime.php is written by the Symfony Runtime component
// Symfony (the symfony/runtime library): it loads the classes, reads the
// .env file, enables debug mode, and then calls the function below, which renders the
// application core; finally, it has the core process the current request, sends the
// response, and completes the request (see the index.php file in the examples)

use App\Kernel;

require_once dirname(__DIR__).'/vendor/autoload_runtime.php';

return function (array $context) {
    return new Kernel($context['APP_ENV'], (bool) $context['APP_DEBUG']);
};

The entry point for the examples (Example 01) loaded the classes, read the file [.env], enabled debug mode, created the core, had it process the request, sent the response, and terminated the request. All of this is handled here by the [Runtime] component of [Symfony] (line 14): this is the form of the [public/index.php] file in a standard [Symfony] application.

  • Line 14: The file [vendor/autoload_runtime.php], written by [Composer] (see [composer.json]), loads the class loader, then executes the script that included it, in this case, [public/index.php], to obtain its return value: an included [PHP] file can return a value ([return]), just like a function;
  • Lines 16–18: This value is an anonymous function that receives the application context (the environment variables, read from [.env] by the [Runtime] component) and returns the core. The [Runtime] component handles the rest: the [Request], [handle], [send], and [terminate] objects.

The advantage of this approach is that the same [index.php] works with servers other than [PHP-FPM]. With the worker mode of [FrankenPHP] (see the section on scopes), for example, a different “runtime” keeps the kernel in memory and has it process requests sequentially, without this file changing. The file [bin/console] has the same structure: its function handles the execution of commands, built around the kernel.

docs.title: 11.7.2. src/Kernel.php and config/services.yaml
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Kernel.php: the application core (see Example 01)

namespace App;

use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Kernel\MicroKernelTrait;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Kernel as BaseKernel;

class Kernel extends BaseKernel
{
    use MicroKernelTrait;

    public function boot(): void
    {
        parent::boot();
         // the time zone: that of the doctor’s office. It sets the current date (not
         // for appointments in the past; see src/Metier/Dates.php)
        date_default_timezone_set('Europe/Paris');
    }
}

The core of the examples (Example 01), with one additional method:

  • lines 13–19: [boot] is called when the kernel starts up, for each request. It sets the time zone for [PHP]. By default, [PHP] operates in the time zone specified in its configuration ([date.timezone], in the file [php.ini]), which is often Coordinated Universal Time (UTC); however, the current date is used for a business rule: no appointments in the past. In Paris, between midnight and 2:00 a.m. in the summer, the day UTC is still the previous day: the firm’s time zone takes precedence.
# =========================================================================
# config/services.yaml: the application’s SERVICES (see Example 06). All
# classes in the src/ directory are declared to the container, which creates them on demand and
# provides each one with the objects it needs (dependency injection): a
# controller receives the ApplicationModel, which receives the business layer, which receives the
# DAO, which receive the Doctrine entity manager...
# Only one object of each class per query.
# =========================================================================
services:
    _defaults:
        autowire: true
        autoconfigure: true

    App\:
        resource: '../src/'
         # Objects of type DONNÉES, created by code (or by Doctrine), never by the
         # container: these are not services
        exclude:
            - '../src/Entity/'
            - '../src/Domain/'
            - '../src/Vues/'
            - '../src/Kernel.php'
  • Lines 10–15: All classes in the [src] folder are services created by the container, which provides each one with the objects it requests in its constructor (example 06). The services are shared: a single [ApplicationModel], a single [MetierService]... for the entire request (see the chapter on scopes);
  • lines 16–22: except for data classes: entities created by [Doctrine] or by the business layer, calculated calendar objects, and view models created by actions. These are excluded: they are not services. (Other data classes, such as [DonneesPersonne] or [Message], are declared, but since no one requests them from the container, the container discards them on its own.)

There is nothing else to declare: the listeners ([#[AsEventListener]]), the controllers ([#[Route]]), the extensions [Twig], the form types, and the authenticator are recognized by the container based on their attributes or their parent class ([autoconfigure]), and configured accordingly. The command [php bin/console debug:container App] lists the application’s services.

docs.title: 11.8. The entities
docs.text: The [Doctrine] entities (Example 28): one class per table, in the [src/Entity] folder.

docs.title: 11.8.1. src/Entity/Role.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Role.php: a user’s three roles (column users.role):
//    - ADMI N: the administrator—schedules appointments and manages doctors and clients;
//    - DOCTOR: a doctor—books and cancels appointments;
//    - USE  R : a client (patient)—books appointments for themselves, manages their account.
// A “backed” enum: each case has a value, the string
// is stored as-is in the database; Role::from('ADMIN') performs the reverse process.

namespace App\Entity;

enum Role: string
{
    case ADMIN = 'ADMIN';
    case DOCTOR = 'DOCTOR';
    case USER = 'USER';

     // The role as defined by Symfony (see config/packages/security.yaml): ROLE_ADMIN...
    public function roleSymfony(): string
    {
        return 'ROLE_'.$this->value;
    }
}

The three roles, listed as follows ([enum], [PHP] 8.1): a type whose only possible values are its cases: [Role::ADMIN], [Role::DOCTOR], and [Role::USER]. A variable of type [Role] cannot contain ['ADMINN']: the typo is detected. [enum Role: string] declares a backed enumeration: each case has a value, in this case the base-sorted string. [Role::ADMIN->value] is equal to ['ADMIN']; [Role::from('ADMIN')] returns the corresponding case (and throws an exception for an unknown value); [Role::tryFrom(...)] returns [null] in this case. An enumeration can have methods: [roleSymfony()] (lines 18–21) returns the role as defined by [Symfony], [ROLE_ADMIN], [ROLE_DOCTOR], or [ROLE_USER] (example 25)—the one verified by the rules [access_control]. [$this] designates the case here.

docs.title: 11.8.2. src/Entity/User.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Entity/User.php: a user authorized to log in (table [users]).
// Each doctor and each client has a SON account (column [user] in the tables
// [medecins] and [clients]; see Personne.php).
//
// Uniqueness constraint SQL: unq_users_login (a login belongs to only one
// account). It is created by the script database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql; the
// business layer recognizes it by its NOM (see src/Metier/MetierService.php).
//
// PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface: a user with a (hashed) password;
// this is what the Symfony hashing service expects (see AuthService).
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Core\User\PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'users')]
class User implements PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface
{
     #[ORM\Id]
     #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
     #[ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

     // the version number of the line: the optimistic lock (see example 28)
     #[ORM\Version]
     #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    private int $version = 0;

    public function __construct(
         #[ORM\Column(length: 30)]
        private string $login,
         // the password HACHÉ (bcrypt), never the password itself
         #[ORM\Column(length: 100)]
        private string $password,
         // the display name after logging in: "Marie PELISSIER"
         #[ORM\Column(length: 40)]
        private string $nom,
         // enumType: the column (text) becomes a Role, and vice versa
         #[ORM\Column(length: 10, enumType: Role::class)]
        private Role $role,
    ) {
    }

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getVersion(): int
    {
        return $this->version;
    }

    public function getLogin(): string
    {
        return $this->login;
    }

    public function getPassword(): string
    {
        return $this->password;
    }

    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return $this->nom;
    }

    public function getRole(): Role
    {
        return $this->role;
    }

    public function setLogin(string $login): void
    {
        $this->login = $login;
    }

    public function setPassword(string $hachage): void
    {
        $this->password = $hachage;
    }

    public function setNom(string $nom): void
    {
        $this->nom = $nom;
    }
}
  • lines 21–23: the entity in table [users]. It implements the [PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface] interface of the security component (Example 25): this is what the password hashing service expects;
  • lines 25–33: the primary key and version, the optimistic lock (Example 28);
  • lines 35–48: the other columns are declared in the constructor using constructor promotion (Example 03): the attributes [#[ORM\Column]] can be applied to both a promoted parameter and a property. [length] specifies the length of the [VARCHAR] columns. Line 45: The option [enumType] converts the column [role] (text) to [Role] during read operations, and vice versa during write operations: [$user->getRole()] returns a [Role], never a string;
  • Lines 50–93: the getters and three setter methods. The primary key and the version do not have setter methods: [Doctrine] keeps them up to date.

docs.title: 11.8.3. src/Entity/Personne.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Entity/Personne.php: what doctors (table [medecins]) and
// clients (table [clients]) have in common: a title, a last name, a first name—and the associated
// associated user account (column [user]).
//
// Both tables have exactly the same columns: they are described UNE times,
// in this class ABSTRAITE (a “Person” is never created), from which
// "Doctor" and "Client"; each specifies only the name of its table.
// #[ORM\MappedSuperclass]: a parent class whose columns are those of the
// entities that inherit from it, but which has no table of its own.
//
// Note: [Client] refers here to a PATIENT from the medical practice, not a client
// HTTP! This is the vocabulary from the original business domain, preserved as-is.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\MappedSuperclass]
abstract class Personne
{
     #[ORM\Id]
     #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
     #[ORM\Column]
    protected ?int $id = null;

     // optimistic lock (see Example 28)
     #[ORM\Version]
     #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    protected int $version = 0;

    public function __construct(
         // Mr., Mrs., Ms.
         #[ORM\Column(length: 5)]
        protected string $titre,
         #[ORM\Column(length: 20)]
        protected string $nom,
         #[ORM\Column(length: 20)]
        protected string $prenom,
        // -------------------------------------------------------------------
         // The RELATION user account: a person has the UN account,
         // identified by the foreign key [user]. #[ORM\OneToOne]: one account per
         // person, one person per account; #[ORM\JoinColumn]: the column for the
         // foreign key (surrounded by grave accents: `user` is a keyword in the
         // SQL of MySQL). $medecin->getCompte() returns a User object, retrieved from the database on the
         // first access—or upon the request, if it requires it (see src/Dao)
        // -------------------------------------------------------------------
         #[ORM\OneToOne]
         #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: '`user`', nullable: false)]
        protected User $compte,
    ) {
    }

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getVersion(): int
    {
        return $this->version;
    }

    public function getTitre(): string
    {
        return $this->titre;
    }

    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return $this->nom;
    }

    public function getPrenom(): string
    {
        return $this->prenom;
    }

    public function getCompte(): User
    {
        return $this->compte;
    }

    public function modifier(string $titre, string $nom, string $prenom): void
    {
        $this->titre = $titre;
        $this->nom = $nom;
        $this->prenom = $prenom;
    }

     // "Ms. Alice DURAND"
    public function libelle(): string
    {
        return "{$this->titre} {$this->prenom} {$this->nom}";
    }
}

The tables [medecins] and [clients] have the same columns. Their shared description is written once, in an abstract class ([abstract class]): a class for which no objects are ever created, serving only as a base class for inheritance. The classes [Medecin] and [Client] inherit from it.

  • Line 22: The attribute [#[ORM\MappedSuperclass]] makes the class a superclass: its columns are those of each of the entities that inherit from it, but it does not have its own table. ([Doctrine] also supports true entity hierarchies, organized in a single table or in one table per class: this is not the case here, where the two tables are independent.) The properties are [protected]: visible to child classes;
  • Lines 51–53: The relationship to the account. [#[ORM\OneToOne]]: A person has an account, and an account belongs to at most one person. [#[ORM\JoinColumn]] refers to the foreign key column, [user], and ensures that it is not empty ([nullable: false]). The column name is enclosed in grave accents: [user] is a word in the language SQL of [MySQL], and [Doctrine] will enclose it in this way in the SQL commands it writes (see the console output above). The property [compte] is a [User] object, not a number: that is the purpose of a ORM. When [Doctrine] reads a person, it also reads their account if the request calls for it (lazy loading; see the DAO layer); otherwise, it places a lazy [User] object (lazy) in the property, which will only be read from the database upon the first access to one of its properties—except for its ID, which it already knows;
  • lines 87–92: modification of the three identity columns;
  • lines 95–98: the name of a person, “Ms. Alice DURAND,” used by all pages. In a string enclosed in quotation marks, [{$this->titre}] inserts the value of a property.

docs.title: 11.8.4. src/Entity/Medecin.php and Client.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Medecin.php: a doctor (table [medecins]).

docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Creneau.php: a doctor’s time slot (table [creneaux]):
// 8:00 a.m. – 8:20 a.m., etc. The time slots are created by the script SQL: the application does not
// simply reads them.

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'creneaux')]
class Creneau
{
     #[ORM\Id]
     #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
     #[ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

     #[ORM\Version]
     #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    private int $version = 0;

     // multiple time slots for the same doctor: #[ORM\ManyToOne], by the key
     // foreign key [id_medecin]
     #[ORM\ManyToOne]
     #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: 'id_medecin', nullable: false)]
    private Medecin $medecin;

     #[ORM\Column]
    private int $hdebut;

     #[ORM\Column]
    private int $mdebut;

     #[ORM\Column]
    private int $hfin;

     #[ORM\Column]
    private int $mfin;

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getMedecin(): Medecin
    {
        return $this->medecin;
    }

     // "8:00 - 8:20"; sprintf('%02d'): "8:05" instead of "8:5"
    public function horaire(): string
    {
        return sprintf('%d:%02d - %d:%02d', $this->hdebut, $this->mdebut, $this->hfin, $this->mfin);
    }
}
  • lines 26–28: the relationship to the doctor for the time slot. [#[ORM\ManyToOne]]: multiple time slots for the same doctor, via the foreign key [id_medecin];
  • lines 30–40: the start and end hours and minutes. The time slots are created by the script SQL: the class has no constructor, and [Doctrine] populates its properties itself;
  • lines 53–56: the time range, “8:00 – 8:20.” The [%02d] format of [sprintf] writes a two-digit integer, padded with zeros: [8:05] rather than [8:5].

docs.title: 11.8.6. src/Entity/Rv.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Rv.php: an appointment (table [rv]): a client, in a time slot, on a
// given day.
// Uniqueness constraint SQL: unq1_rv (day, id_creneau)—a time slot is reserved
// only once per day. Created by the SQL script, identified by its name in the
// business layer.

namespace App\Entity;

use DateTimeImmutable;
use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'rv')]
class Rv
{
     #[ORM\Id]
     #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
     #[ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

     #[ORM\Version]
     #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    private int $version = 0;

    public function __construct(
         // the type date_immutable: the column [jour] (type SQL DATE) becomes a date
         // DateTimeImmutable, at midnight; it is written in the yyyy-mm-dd format
         #[ORM\Column(type: Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE)]
        private DateTimeImmutable $jour,
         #[ORM\ManyToOne]
         #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: 'id_creneau', nullable: false)]
        private Creneau $creneau,
         #[ORM\ManyToOne]
         #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: 'id_client', nullable: false)]
        private Client $client,
    ) {
    }

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getJour(): DateTimeImmutable
    {
        return $this->jour;
    }

    public function getCreneau(): Creneau
    {
        return $this->creneau;
    }

    public function getClient(): Client
    {
        return $this->client;
    }
}
  • lines 30–31: the column [jour] (type SQL [DATE]) is converted to [DateTimeImmutable] at midnight (type [Doctrine] [date_immutable]). Immutable: its methods never modify the object; they return a new one ([$jour->modify('+1 day')] returns the next day, [$jour] remains unchanged). The entire application works with immutable dates: a date shared among multiple objects cannot be modified by one of them without the others’ knowledge;
  • lines 32–37: two relationships, one to the time slot and one to the appointment’s client.

Two calculated objects that do not correspond to any table: a time slot and its potential appointment on a given day; a doctor’s calendar for a single day, listing their available time slots. These are [readonly] classes (example 03), whose properties are declared in the constructor. The comment [/** @param list<CreneauMedecinJour> ... */] specifies the contents of the array: [PHP] cannot determine the type of an array’s contents, but editors ([PHP Intelephense]) and analysis tools read these comments, known as [PHPDoc].

docs.title: 11.10. The DAO layer
docs.text: The DAO layer (Example 28) groups together the queries: one class per table, with no business logic. Its methods do not start a transaction; the business layer calls them within its own transactions. They are written in DQL (Example 28), or using the query builder in [Doctrine], which generates a DQL query through method calls; the values are query parameters: SQL injection is not possible.

docs.title: 11.10.1. src/Dao/PersonneDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Dao/PersonneDao.php: the DAO layer shared by doctors and clients.
//
// The DAO for doctors and clients would be identical: this ABSTRAITE
// is written only once. $this->class is the class of the entity in question
// (Doctor::class or Client::class): DQL queries target the SA table.
//
// Queries are written in DQL, Doctrine’s query language (see
// example 28), which Doctrine translates into SQL. The values (first name, last name...) are
// PARAMÈTRES from the query (:first_name): no string concatenation, so no
// SQL injection. These methods do not open any transactions: it is the
// business layer that calls them, within its own transactions.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Personne;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;
use Doctrine\ORM\QueryBuilder;

abstract class PersonneDao
{
     /** @param class-string<Person> $classe */
    public function __construct(protected EntityManagerInterface $em, protected string $classe)
    {
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // a query on the class table, including the user account. The
     // CONSTRUCTEUR DE REQUÊTES from Doctrine (createQueryBuilder) generates the query
     // DQL via method calls:
        // SELECT p, c FROM App\Entity\Medecin p JOIN p.compte c
     // JOIN p.compte c: the join SQL with the table [users]; SELECT p, c: the
     // accounts are loaded PAR LA MÊME query. Otherwise, each access to
     // $personne->getCompte() would trigger its own query
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    protected function requete(): QueryBuilder
    {
        return $this->em->createQueryBuilder()
            ->select('p', 'c')
            ->from($this->classe, 'p')
            ->join('p.compte', 'c');
    }

     // list sorted by last name, then first name
     /** @return list<Person> */
    public function lister(): array
    {
        return $this->requete()->orderBy('p.nom')->addOrderBy('p.prenom')->getQuery()->getResult();
    }

     // a person and their account; null if they do not exist
    public function lire(int $id): ?Personne
    {
        return $this->requete()->where('p.id = :id')->setParameter('id', $id)
            ->getQuery()->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

     // the person whose user account is [$idUser]
    public function lireParUser(int $idUser): ?Personne
    {
        return $this->requete()->where('c.id = :idUser')->setParameter('idUser', $idUser)
            ->getQuery()->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

     // the person with this first and last name, if such a person exists. The comparison is
     // performed by MySQL, i.e., using the database’s collation (utf8mb4_unicode_ci: without
     // taking into account capital letters or accents)—exactly the same rule as
     // the one for the uniqueness constraint SQL
    public function homonyme(string $prenom, string $nom): ?Personne
    {
        return $this->requete()->where('p.prenom = :prenom')->andWhere('p.nom = :nom')
            ->setParameter('prenom', $prenom)->setParameter('nom', $nom)
            ->setMaxResults(1)->getQuery()->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

     // the record will be inserted during the next flush (that of the
     // business layer); the database will generate its ID, which Doctrine will store in the object
    public function ajouter(Personne $personne): void
    {
        $this->em->persist($personne);
    }

     // the person will be deleted by the next flush
    public function supprimer(Personne $personne): void
    {
        $this->em->remove($personne);
    }
}

The DAO layer common to both doctors and clients, implemented once in an abstract class.

  • Line 25: The constructor receives the entity manager (Example 28) and the relevant class, [Medecin::class] or [Client::class] (a string representing the full class name). The comment [@param class-string<Personne>] clarifies this for developers. The service container does not know which string to provide: it is the child classes that call this constructor;
  • lines 38–44: a query that also loads the accounts of the read users. [createQueryBuilder] creates a query builder; [select('p', 'c')], [from($this->classe, 'p')], and [join('p.compte', 'c')] write the query DQL [SELECT p, c FROM App\Entity\Medecin p JOIN p.compte c]. The join ([JOIN]) follows the relationship [compte] of the entity: [Doctrine] derives the condition SQL ([ON m0_.user = u1_.id]). The [SELECT] for both aliases requires eager loading of the accounts: a single query retrieves the people and their accounts. Without it, the list of doctors displayed by the administrator would trigger one query per doctor upon the first access to [$medecin->getCompte()->getLogin()]: this is the so-called “N + 1 queries” problem. Another reason: the lists of doctors and clients are stored in the cache ([ApplicationModel], discussed later); the objects added to the cache must be complete;
  • lines 48–51: the list, sorted by last name then first name ([orderBy], then [addOrderBy]: a second criterion; a second [orderBy] would replace the first). [getQuery()] returns the query DQL; [getResult()] executes it and returns the array of entities;
  • lines 54–58: [where] adds a condition with a named parameter ([:id]), whose value is provided by [setParameter]. [getOneOrNullResult] returns the single entity found, or [null];
  • lines 61–65: the person whose account is [$idUser], condition based on the linked account ID;
  • lines 71–76: the person with the same first and last names. [andWhere] adds a second condition (a second [where] would replace the first). The comparison is performed by [MySQL], using the database’s collation: case-insensitive and ignoring accents, exactly like the uniqueness constraint (Example 28);
  • lines 80–89: the insertion and deletion, which will be sent to the database by [flush] as part of the business layer transaction (Example 28).

There is no update method: the business layer modifies the read entity, and [Doctrine] will send [UPDATE] to [flush] (change tracking, Example 28), using an optimistic lock.

docs.title: 11.10.2. src/Dao/MedecinDao.php and ClientDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Dao/MedecinDao.php: the DAO for doctors—everything is inherited from PersonneDao.

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Medecin;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class MedecinDao extends PersonneDao
{
    public function __construct(EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
        parent::__construct($em, Medecin::class);
    }
}

Everything is inherited: the constructor receives the container’s entity manager and passes it to [PersonneDao] along with the entity class ([parent::__construct] calls the parent class’s constructor).

<?php
// src/Dao/ClientDao.php: the DAO for clients—the one for people, plus a
// locking method.

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Client;
use Doctrine\DBAL\LockMode;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class ClientDao extends PersonneDao
{
    public function __construct(EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
        parent::__construct($em, Client::class);
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // places a VERROU on a customer’s line until the end of the transaction in
     // progress (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), and returns its ID (null if the client does
     // does not exist). A second transaction that requests the same lock ATTEND as the
     // first one must be completed. LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE: the "pessimistic" lock
     // in Doctrine, which requires an open transaction.
     // Used for scheduling appointments (see MetierService::ajouterRv): two
     // simultaneous appointments for the same patient are thus processed—one
     // APRÈS the other, and the second reservation sees the appointment created by the first.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public function verrouiller(int $id): ?int
    {
        $ligne = $this->em->createQuery('SELECT c.id FROM App\Entity\Client c WHERE c.id = :id')
            ->setParameter('id', $id)
            ->setLockMode(LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
            ->getOneOrNullResult();
        return $ligne['id'] ?? null;
    }
}
  • Lines 28–35: a pessimistic lock, the other type of lock. [setLockMode(LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)] adds [FOR UPDATE] to the query: [SELECT c0_.id AS id_0 FROM clients c0_ WHERE c0_.id = ? FOR UPDATE]. The row being read is locked until the end of the current transaction: another transaction requesting the same lock waits for the first one to finish. [Doctrine] denies this lock outside of a transaction. The query reads only the ID ([SELECT c.id]): its result is not an entity, but an associative array ([['id' => 3]]), or [null]. We will see, in the business layer, what this lock is used for.

docs.title: 11.10.3. src/Dao/CreneauDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Dao/CreneauDao.php: DAO layer for time slots.

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Creneau;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class CreneauDao
{
    public function __construct(private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

     // a time slot and its doctor
    public function lire(int $id): ?Creneau
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT c, m FROM App\Entity\Creneau c JOIN c.medecin m WHERE c.id = :id')
            ->setParameter('id', $id)->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

     // a doctor’s time slots, in chronological order. c.medecin = :idMedecin :
     // an association mapped to an ID, that of the foreign key
     /** @return list<Appointment> */
    public function listerParMedecin(int $idMedecin): array
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT c FROM App\Entity\Creneau c WHERE c.medecin = :idMedecin ORDER BY c.hdebut, c.mdebut')
            ->setParameter('idMedecin', $idMedecin)->getResult();
    }

     // deletes all time slots for a doctor (removal of a doctor): a
     // DQL DELETE query, executed immediately:
        // DELETE FROM time slots WHERE id_medecin = ?
    public function supprimerParMedecin(int $idMedecin): void
    {
        $this->em->createQuery('DELETE FROM App\Entity\Creneau c WHERE c.medecin = :idMedecin')
            ->setParameter('idMedecin', $idMedecin)->execute();
    }
}

An appointment slot and its doctor (preloaded); a doctor’s appointment slots, in chronological order: [c.medecin = :idMedecin] compares a relationship to an ID—that of the foreign key; and a [DELETE] written as DQL, executed immediately ([execute()]), without reading the rows first.

docs.title: 11.10.4. src/Dao/RvDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Dao/RvDao.php: DAO layer for appointments.
//
// The [rv] table does not directly reference the doctor: the appointment slot is used as an intermediary
// (JOIN r.creneau cr ... WHERE cr.medecin = ...).
// Dates are passed along with their type (Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE): Doctrine
// written in the database format, yyyy-mm-dd.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Rv;
use DateTimeImmutable;
use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class RvDao
{
    public function __construct(private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

     // an appointment, its client, and its time slot
    public function lire(int $id): ?Rv
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT r, cl, cr FROM App\Entity\Rv r JOIN r.client cl JOIN r.creneau cr WHERE r.id = :id')
            ->setParameter('id', $id)->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

     // a doctor’s appointments on a given day, along with their clients
     /** @return list<Rv> */
    public function rvMedecinJour(int $idMedecin, DateTimeImmutable $jour): array
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
             'SELECT r, cl FROM App\Entity\Rv r JOIN r.client cl JOIN r.creneau cr
             WHERE r.jour = :jour AND cr.medecin = :idMedecin')
            ->setParameter('jour', $jour, Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE)
            ->setParameter('idMedecin', $idMedecin)
            ->getResult();
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // a client’s appointments starting from day [$depuis] (inclusive), in
     // chronological order, with the time slot ET and the doctor assigned to that slot (two joins:
     // JOIN r.creneau cr JOIN cr.medecin m, and SELECT r, cr, m)
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     /** @return list<Rv> */
    public function rvAVenirClient(int $idClient, DateTimeImmutable $depuis): array
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
             'SELECT r, cr, m FROM App\Entity\Rv r JOIN r.creneau cr JOIN cr.medecin m
             WHERE r.client = :idClient AND r.jour >= :depuis
             ORDER BY r.jour, cr.hdebut, cr.mdebut')
            ->setParameter('idClient', $idClient)
            ->setParameter('depuis', $depuis, Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE)
            ->getResult();
    }

     // number of appointments for a client starting on day [$depuis] (inclusive);
     // getSingleScalarResult: the single value in the single row of the result
    public function compterAVenirClient(int $idClient, DateTimeImmutable $depuis): int
    {
        return (int) $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT COUNT(r.id) FROM App\Entity\Rv r WHERE r.client = :idClient AND r.jour >= :depuis')
            ->setParameter('idClient', $idClient)
            ->setParameter('depuis', $depuis, Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE)
            ->getSingleScalarResult();
    }

     // number of appointments (past or future) for a doctor
    public function compterParMedecin(int $idMedecin): int
    {
        return (int) $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT COUNT(r.id) FROM App\Entity\Rv r JOIN r.creneau cr WHERE cr.medecin = :idMedecin')
            ->setParameter('idMedecin', $idMedecin)
            ->getSingleScalarResult();
    }

     // the appointment will be inserted during the next flush
    public function ajouter(Rv $rv): void
    {
        $this->em->persist($rv);
    }

    public function supprimer(Rv $rv): void
    {
        $this->em->remove($rv);
    }

     // deletes TOUS a client’s appointments (past and future) immediately
    public function supprimerParClient(int $idClient): void
    {
        $this->em->createQuery('DELETE FROM App\Entity\Rv r WHERE r.client = :idClient')
            ->setParameter('idClient', $idClient)->execute();
    }
}

The table [rv] does not directly reference the doctor: it goes through the time slot.

  • Lines 34–42: a doctor’s appointments on a given day, and their clients. Two joins: one ([r.client cl]) to load the clients ([SELECT r, cl]), the other ([r.creneau cr]) for the filter on the doctor. The third parameter of [setParameter] specifies the value type [Doctrine]: a [DateTimeImmutable] is then written in the column format [DATE], [aaaa-mm-jj];
  • lines 50–59: a patient’s upcoming appointments, with their time slot and the doctor assigned to that slot: [JOIN cr.medecin m] follows a relationship from the relation. Sorting is also performed based on the time slot, a column from another table: this is made possible by the join;
  • lines 63–79: counts. [COUNT(r.id)] counts the appointments; [getSingleScalarResult] returns the single value from the single row in the result (a string, converted to an integer by [(int)]);
  • lines 93–97: Deleting all appointments for a client, using DQL.

docs.text:
<?php
// src/Dao/UserDao.php: DAO layer for user accounts. Create (or delete)
// a doctor or a client also creates (or deletes) their account—see src/Metier.
// A modified account is updated via its methods (setLogin...): Doctrine will send
// the UPDATE on the next flush (tracking changes; see Example 28).

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\User;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class UserDao
{
    public function __construct(private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

     // null if no user has this login; findOneBy: the entity's repository
     // searches for the row whose columns have these values
    public function lireParLogin(string $login): ?User
    {
        return $this->em->getRepository(User::class)->findOneBy(['login' => $login]);
    }

    public function ajouter(User $user): void
    {
        $this->em->persist($user);
    }

    public function supprimer(User $user): void
    {
        $this->em->remove($user);
    }
