docs.title: 11.21. Static files
docs.text: The [public] folder is the site’s root directory: the server sends the files located there as-is (example 15). In addition to [index.php], it contains [Bootstrap] ([lib/bootstrap]), a stylesheet, and a script.

docs.title: 11.21.1. public/css/styles.css
docs.text:
/* =========================================================================
   public/css/styles.css - quelques réglages en plus de Bootstrap
   (les mêmes que dans les autres versions de cette application).
   ========================================================================= */

body {
  background-color: #f5f7fa;
}

.creneau-libre:hover {
  background-color: #e9f7ef;
}

/* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
   .zone-erreur : les messages d'erreur, en bas de page, sur fond rose léger
   (cf. templates/fragments/erreurs.html.twig).
   position: sticky + bottom : si la page est plus haute que la fenêtre (un
   agenda de 12 créneaux, par exemple), la zone reste collée au bas de la
   fenêtre au lieu de disparaître sous la ligne de flottaison - sans jamais
   recouvrir le contenu quand la page est courte.
   z-index : au-dessus du fond grisé de la fenêtre de réservation (.modal-backdrop).
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
.zone-erreur {
  position: sticky;
  bottom: 1rem;
  z-index: 1060;
  margin-top: 1.5rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  background-color: #fdecef; /* light pink */
  border: 1px solid #f5c2c7;
  border-radius: 0.375rem;
  color: #842029;
}

/* the two main options on the patient’s “My Account” page */
.carte-option {
  transition: border-color 0.15s, box-shadow 0.15s;
}

.carte-option:hover {
  border-color: #0d6efd;
  box-shadow: 0 0.25rem 0.75rem rgba(13, 110, 253, 0.15);
}

/* the CAPTCHA image (SVG, 150 x 50 pixels) */
.captcha-image svg {
  display: block;
  border: 1px solid #dee2e6;
  border-radius: 0.375rem;
}

A few additional settings for [Bootstrap], the same as in the other versions of the application.

  • Lines 10–12: A bookable row in the calendar turns green when the mouse hovers over it;
  • lines 23–33: the error area at the bottom of the page has a light pink background. [position: sticky] with [bottom: 1rem]: if the page is taller than the window (a calendar with 12 time slots), the area remains anchored to the bottom of the window instead of disappearing below the scroll bar; if the page is short, it stays in place without covering anything. [z-index]: It appears over the gray background of the booking window;
  • lines 36–43: the two large “My Account” cards, which light up when the mouse hovers over them;
  • lines 46–50: the CAPTCHA image, with a border.

docs.title: 11.21.2. public/js/app.js
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// public/js/app.js - the application's SEUL JavaScript.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The entire application works without JavaScript. This script adds a
// convenience feature: before submitting a form that includes the
// data-confirmation="...", a modal window asks "Are you sure?"
// (the window itself is located in the page: templates/fragments/confirmation.html.twig).
// If JavaScript is disabled, the form simply submits without
// confirmation—nothing breaks (the principle of “progressive enhancement”).
//
// Why not window.confirm()? Its input field doesn’t format properly, and its
// buttons remain in the browser’s language, not the page’s.
// =========================================================================

(() => {
  const modale = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation');
  if (!modale) {
    return;
  }
  const message = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation-message');
  const boutonNon = modale.querySelector('.modal-footer [data-action="non"]');

  let formulaireEnAttente = null; // the form to submit if you confirm
  let focusPrecedent = null; // the element to focus on when closing

  function ouvrir(formulaire) {
    formulaireEnAttente = formulaire;
    focusPrecedent = document.activeElement;
     // textContent (not innerHTML): the message is displayed as TEXTE,
     // never interpreted as HTML
    message.textContent = formulaire.dataset.confirmation;
    modale.classList.remove('d-none');
     // the focus moves to "No": accidentally pressing Enter does not delete anything
    boutonNon.focus();
  }

  function fermer() {
    modale.classList.add('d-none');
    formulaireEnAttente = null;
    if (focusPrecedent) {
      focusPrecedent.focus();
    }
  }

   // 1. We intercept the submission of forms requiring confirmation
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((formulaire) => {
    formulaire.addEventListener('submit', (evenement) => {
      evenement.preventDefault();
      ouvrir(formulaire);
    });
  });

   // 2. The window’s buttons (Yes / No / close button)
  modale.addEventListener('click', (evenement) => {
    const action = evenement.target.closest('[data-action]')?.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'oui') {
      const formulaire = formulaireEnAttente;
      fermer();
       // formulaire.submit() submits the form SANS to trigger again
       // the 'submit' event: no new confirmation request
      formulaire.submit();
    } else if (action === 'non') {
      fermer();
    } else if (evenement.target.classList.contains('modal')) {
      fermer(); // Click on the grayed-out background, outside the window
    }
  });

   // 3. Keyboard: Esc closes the window; Tab keeps the focus on the window
   /   / (otherwise, the focus would move to the grayed-out page behind it)
  modale.addEventListener('keydown', (evenement) => {
    if (evenement.key === 'Escape') {
      fermer();
    } else if (evenement.key === 'Tab') {
      const boutons = [...modale.querySelectorAll('button')];
      const premier = boutons[0];
      const dernier = boutons[boutons.length - 1];
      if (evenement.shiftKey && document.activeElement === premier) {
        evenement.preventDefault();
        dernier.focus();
      } else if (!evenement.shiftKey && document.activeElement === dernier) {
        evenement.preventDefault();
        premier.focus();
      }
    }
  });
})();

The only [JavaScript] in the application—the one from Example 21—with a few additions. The entire application works without [JavaScript]: this script adds convenience by providing a confirmation before submitting a form that carries the [data-confirmation] attribute. If [JavaScript] is disabled, the form submits without confirmation: nothing breaks (principle of progressive enhancement).

  • Lines 15–19: The script is a function called as soon as it is defined ([(() => { ... })()]); its variables are not visible to the rest of the page. Without a confirmation window on the page, it does nothing;
  • Lines 26–35: Opening the window: the form to be submitted if the user confirms is stored, and the form’s message is displayed in the window. [textContent], not [innerHTML]: the message is displayed as text and is never interpreted as HTML. Focus moves to the “No” button: accidentally pressing Enter does not delete anything;
  • lines 37–43: closing the window; focus returns to the element that had it previously;
  • lines 46–51: the submission of each form to be confirmed is intercepted ([preventDefault] prevents it), and the window opens;
  • lines 54–67: the window’s buttons. A single handler for the entire window: [closest('[data-action]')] finds the clicked button or the element containing it. “Yes” submits the form via [formulaire.submit()], which does not trigger the [submit] event: no new confirmation request is issued. Clicking on the grayed-out background outside the window closes it;
  • lines 71–86: the keyboard. Esc closes the window; the Tab key moves focus from one button to another without leaving the window (otherwise, it would move to the grayed-out page behind it): this is what users who navigate with the keyboard and screen readers expect.

docs.title: 12. Conclusion
docs.text:
This document described the development of a MVC web application using the [Symfony] framework: an application whose HTML pages are generated by the server, using [Twig] views, without a browser-side [JavaScript] framework. He followed the [Laravel] course step by step, which itself builds upon the courses [Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS]: actions and routing to views, forms, internationalization, security, and data access, followed by a comprehensive case study.

The same 28 examples and the same application were thus written using six frameworks: in [TypeScript], in [C#], in [Java], in [Python], and twice in [PHP]. The concepts are the same; only the names and mechanisms differ. The correspondences between [Laravel] and [Symfony], the two major frameworks of the [PHP] world:

[Laravel][Symfony][bootstrap/app.php], service providers,([src/Kernel.php]), bundles, compiled container ([config/services.yaml], [#[Autowire]])[composer.json], folder [vendor], [php artisan][composer.json], folder [vendor], [php bin/console]file [.env], folder [config] (files [PHP]), functions [env] and [config]file [.env], folder [config/packages] (files YAML), [%env(...)%], container settings[routes/web.php], named routes, route groupscontroller attributes [#[Route]], on the action and on the class[view], [redirect], [route][render], [redirectToRoute], [generateUrl] ([AbstractController]); [path] in viewsobject [Request], constraints ([whereNumber]), model linkobject [Request], [requirements] ([{id<\d+>}]), argument resolvers, [#[MapQueryString]], [#[MapRequestPayload]][Validator], form requests ([FormRequest]), rules, [$errors], [old()]Validator component (attribute constraints), Form component (types, [handleRequest], [isValid])views [Blade], [{{ }}], [@foreach], [@if]views [Twig], [{{ }}], [{% for %}], [{% if %}][@extends] and sections, [@include], components ([<x-...>])[{% extends %}] and blocks, [{% include %}], macrosview composer ([View::composer])global variables of [Twig], extensions [Twig] (functions, filters)session flash data ([session()->flash], [with])flash messages ([addFlash], [app.flashes]), session in files(global, group, route), [terminate] methodkernel event listeners ([kernel.request], [kernel.controller], [kernel.response], [kernel.terminate]...)[withExceptions], [render], [abort]Earbuds: [kernel.exception], [HttpException], [createNotFoundException]guards ([Auth::viaRequest]), middleware [auth], [Gate], facade [Hash]firewall, authenticators, [access_control], [#[IsGranted]], voters, hashing ([security.yaml])[PreventRequestForgery] middleware, [@csrf] directive (419 response)Form component token, [csrf_token()] and [isCsrfTokenValid] (403 response, or 419 in our application)[RateLimiter] (facade)Component [RateLimiter] (limiters declared in [framework.yaml])folder [lang], function [__()], [App::setLocale]folder [translations] (YAML, ICU), filter [trans], [TranslatorInterface], query language[Carbon] ([isoFormat]), [Number]Extension [intl]: [IntlDateFormatter], [NumberFormatter]Cache ([Cache], [Cache::lock])Cache component (PSR-6 and contracts), Lock component[Eloquent]: Active Record models, relationships ([belongsTo], [with])[Doctrine]: Data Mapper entities, entity manager, DQL and QueryBuilder, relationships ([ManyToOne], [OneToOne])[DB::transaction(...)][wrapInTransaction(...)], [flush][WHERE version = ?] and [version + 1], written to layer DAO[#[ORM\Version]], managed by [Doctrine] ([OptimisticLockException])[php artisan serve][php -S localhost:8000 -t public], or [symfony server:start]

Regarding [Laravel], the key points to note are:

  • [Symfony] is a set of independent components, assembled into bundles. Each component is self-contained, and [Laravel] uses several of them ([HttpFoundation], [HttpKernel], [Routing], [Console]...) : Readers of the previous lesson will recognize the same objects here: [Request] and [Response]. An application named [Symfony] installs only the components it needs: the examples started with just [framework-bundle], and then added, one by one, [Twig], validation, forms, security, and [Doctrine];
  • Everything goes through the service container and dependency injection: no facades or global functions, but services passed to the constructor and declared by type (autowiring). A class’s dependencies are always visible in its constructor. The container is compiled into code [PHP] and cached: this offsets the cost of rebuilding the application with each request (Example 01);
  • The processing of a request consists of a sequence of kernel events to which listeners respond: this is where language, security, application controls (the pass), and error pages are handled. The mechanism is more explicit than the middleware in [Laravel]: each listener chooses its event and priority, and the command [debug:event-dispatcher] displays the order of all listeners;
  • the configuration is explicit, in YAML (or [PHP]) files that describe each bundle: the firewall, access rules, limiters, and session, [Doctrine]. The commands [debug:router], [debug:container], and [debug:config] display what [Symfony] has interpreted;
  • The [PHP] attributes describe the code: roads ([#[Route]]), constraints ([#[Assert\NotBlank]]), entities ([#[ORM\Column]]), listeners ([#[AsEventListener]]), permissions ([#[IsGranted]]), and injection ([#[Autowire]]). We’ve even written some ([#[Chronometre]], [#[PasseInscriptionExige]]);
  • forms are objects, described by classes such as: fields, constraints, value conversion, input redispatch, error messages, and anti-CSRF tokens. This is more code than the form requests in [Laravel] for a small form, and much less for a large one: a theme ([Bootstrap] 5) styles all fields the same way;
  • security is a fully-fledged component: a firewall, authenticators that verify the user, access rules, a role hierarchy, and voters. We adapted it to our needs (a JWT token in a cookie) using an authenticator consisting of a few dozen lines, without losing any of the other features: [access_control], [#[IsGranted]], [is_granted] in the views;
  • [Doctrine] follows the Data Mapper pattern: the entities are ordinary [PHP] objects that are unaware of the database; it is the entity manager that reads them, tracks their changes, and writes them all together, in a single transaction, at the time of the [flush]. More abstract than [Eloquent]’s Active Record, it clearly separates objects from their records and supports mechanisms such as optimistic locking. The SQL order log allows you, as with [Eloquent], to verify what is sent to the database;
  • the [Twig] views have their own language, which is more limited than the [PHP] used in the [Blade] views: a view can only display the data provided to it. This is both a constraint and a guarantee: the logic remains within the classes. They are compiled into [PHP], cached, and automatically escape the content they display.

The case study shows that a classic HTML application, without the essential [JavaScript], remains a simple and robust solution: each page is a URL, the browser’s “Back” button works, and the server controls everything. The limited use of [JavaScript] (confirmation windows) enhances the user experience without being necessary for operation. [Symfony] can also support more interactive applications without leaving [Twig] ([Symfony UX]: [Turbo], [Stimulus], Live Components) or with a browser-side [JavaScript] framework, to which it provides a API JSON ([API Platform]): this will be covered in other documents.

For further information, please refer to the [Symfony] documentation (symfony.com/doc), particularly the pages dedicated to the service container, kernel events, forms, security, and [Doctrine], as well as the documentation for [Twig] (twig.symfony.com), the documentation for [Doctrine] (doctrine-project.org), the documentation for [PHP] (php.net/manual/fr), and compare this application with its counterparts [Laravel], [Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS].

docs.title: 6. Data Scopes
docs.text:
A web application serves many users at once, and each user makes numerous requests. Data can therefore be shared at several levels, known as its scope:

  • application scope: the data is shared by all users throughout the application’s lifetime (the list of doctors, for example);
  • request scope: the data exists only for the duration of processing a request (a view’s model, the logged-in user as identified for that request);
  • session scope: the data is specific to a user and must persist from one request to the next (the selected language, a shopping cart);
  • client scope: data stored in the browser itself, in a cookie.

In [PHP], these scopes behave in a particular way because the application is rebuilt with every request (Example 01): nothing survives in memory from one request to the next. Any data that needs to last longer than a single request is therefore stored outside of [PHP]: in the cache, a database, files, or on the client’s side. This is the so-called “shared-nothing” architecture: each request is processed in isolation by a process that shares nothing with those processing other requests. This approach has significant advantages: an error affects only a single request, no data leaks from one user to another, and multiple identical servers can be run behind a load balancer, provided they share the same cache and database.

In [Symfony], each scope has its own container:

ScopeContainerLifetimeapplicationthe cache (service [cache.app], example 20), or the databasethe selected duration, or unlimitedQuerythe container’s services (one object per class, during the request), the request attributes (example 12)processing a requestsessionthe session ([$request->getSession()], Example 20), maintained by the server and retrieved via a cookieuntil the browser is closed by default, and at most for the duration of the [PHP] session (24 minutes of inactivity by default)clienta cookie ([Cookie::create], example 22), in plain textThe cookie's expiration time

The [Symfony] session is a server-side session, like those for [Java] ([JSESSIONID]) or the standard [PHP], from which it actually borrows the mechanism and the cookie ([PHPSESSID]): its data is stored on the server (one file per session, with the configuration used in our examples), and the browser holds only the identifier—a random number that is impossible to guess. This differs from [Flask], whose entire session is stored in a signed cookie on the client’s side.

docs.title: 6.1.1. The objects: src/Service/CompteurService.php and RequeteInfos.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Service/CompteurService.php: scope APPLICATION, counters shared by
// all requests from all users, stored in the cache (see Example 20)

namespace App\Service;

use Psr\Cache\CacheItemPoolInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Lock\LockFactory;

class CompteurService
{
    public function __construct(
        private CacheItemPoolInterface $cache,
        private LockFactory $verrous,
    ) {
    }

     // one more number under the key [$cle]; the "file" cache does not increment a
     // number atomically: a lock protects read and write operations
    public function suivant(string $cle): int
    {
        $verrou = $this->verrous->createLock("$cle-verrou");
        $verrou->acquire(true);
        try {
            $element = $this->cache->getItem($cle);
            $valeur = ($element->isHit() ? $element->get() : 0) + 1;
            $this->cache->save($element->set($valeur));
            return $valeur;
        } finally {
            $verrou->release();
        }
    }

    public function incrementer(): int
    {
        return $this->suivant('visites');
    }
}
  • lines 12–16: the service receives the application cache and the lock factory (Example 20);
  • lines 20–32: an application-scope counter: a number stored in the cache under a key and incremented by 1 on each call. The “file” cache in our examples does not support atomic increment operations: the value must be read, incremented, and then written, and two concurrent requests could read the same value—resulting in a missed hit. A lock—one per key—therefore protects both read and write operations; the block [finally] releases it in all cases, even after the [return] in line 28;
  • lines 34–37: the visit counter.
<?php
// src/Service/RequeteInfos.php: scope REQUÊTE, the information from a request

namespace App\Service;

use DateTimeImmutable;

class RequeteInfos
{
    public readonly int $numero;

    public readonly string $debut;

     // the container creates a UN object of this class upon the first request, and the
     // then returns it to anyone who requests it during the request
    public function __construct(CompteurService $compteur)
    {
         // a number generated by OBJET, drawn from a counter shared by all requests
        $this->numero = $compteur->suivant('instances');
         // the time, including milliseconds (v)
        $this->debut = (new DateTimeImmutable())->format('H:i:s.v');
    }
}
  • lines 10–12: properties declared as [readonly] one by one (rather than the entire class): they can only be assigned once, by the constructor;
  • lines 16–22: request-scope information: a number, derived from a counter shared by all requests (the previous service, under a different key), and the request time, including milliseconds ([v] format). The constructor receives the [CompteurService] from the container: a service can request another service, just like an action.

No configuration is required: by default, a service in the container is shared (shared). The container creates the object on the first request, then returns the same one to all subsequent requests. In standard [PHP] mode, the container is rebuilt with each request: a shared service is therefore a request-scoped object. (You can also request a new object with each injection using the [shared: false] option in the [services.yaml] file.) A nuance arises with application servers that keep the application in memory from one request to the next to improve performance, such as the worker mode of [FrankenPHP]: in this case, a service is shared by all requests handled by the process. [Symfony] then resets, between requests, the services that implement the [ResetInterface] interface; it is up to those services to ensure that nothing is retained from one request to the next.

docs.title: 6.1.2. A global variable for the views: config/packages/twig.yaml
docs.text:
# config/packages/twig.yaml: the configuration of TwigBundle
twig:
    default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/templates'
     # a GLOBALE variable from the views, which is a SERVICE (the @ denotes a service):
     # the RequeteInfos object of the current request
    globals:
        infos: '@App\Service\RequeteInfos'
  • Lines 6–7: A global variable in the views (Example 15) can be a service: the name of its class, preceded by [@]. All views thus have access to the variable [infos], which is the [RequeteInfos] object of the current request. [Twig] has no equivalent to the [@inject] directive of [Blade]: a view does not request anything from the container; it receives what is given to it.

docs.title: 6.1.3. Signed cookies: src/Service/CookiesSignes.php
docs.text:
A cookie is a piece of data entrusted to the client, which can read and modify it. [Laravel] encrypts its cookies; [Symfony] does not. For a cookie to be trustworthy, however, it simply needs to be signed: its value is transmitted in plaintext, but it is followed by a signature that only the server knows how to calculate, because it depends on a secret key. A value modified by the client no longer has the correct signature, and the server rejects it.

<?php
// src/Service/CookiesSignes.php: SIGNÉS cookies. The value is transmitted in plain text,
// followed by a signature that only the server knows how to calculate: a modified value
// modified by the client no longer has the correct signature and is rejected

namespace App\Service;

use Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Attribute\Autowire;

class CookiesSignes
{
     // the signature key: the application’s secret (APP_SECRET, .env file)
    public function __construct(#[Autowire('%kernel.secret%')] private string $secret)
    {
    }

     // "5" -> "5.3f1c...": the value, a period, the signature (HMAC-SHA256 of the value)
    public function signer(string $valeur): string
    {
        return $valeur.'.'.hash_hmac('sha256', $valeur, $this->secret);
    }

     // the value if the signature is valid, null otherwise
    public function verifier(?string $cookie): ?string
    {
        if ($cookie === null || ! str_contains($cookie, '.')) {
            return null;
        }
         // strrpos: the position of the DERNIER dot
        $valeur = substr($cookie, 0, strrpos($cookie, '.'));
         // hash_equals compares two strings in constant time, which does not reveal
         // how many characters are correct
        return hash_equals($this->signer($valeur), $cookie) ? $valeur : null;
    }
}
  • line 13: The signature key is the application’s secret—the variable [APP_SECRET] in the file [.env] (Example 01)—which the container recognizes as the parameter [kernel.secret]. A parameter is not an object: the attribute [#[Autowire]] tells the container the value to provide, where [%nom%] refers to a parameter;
  • lines 18–21: The signature is HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code): the SHA-256 hash of the value, calculated using the secret key, written in hexadecimal. The cookie contains the value, a period, and then the signature;
  • Lines 24–34: The verification process recalculates the signature of the received value and compares it to the one in the cookie. [hash_equals] compares two strings in a time that does not depend on the number of identical characters: a standard comparison would stop at the first differing character, and an attacker could, by measuring the response time, guess the signature character by character.

This is the principle behind the JWT token, which the next chapter will use for authentication.

docs.title: 6.1.4. The controller: src/Controller/PorteesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/PorteesController.php: the four data ranges

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Service\CompteurService;
use App\Service\CookiesSignes;
use App\Service\RequeteInfos;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Cookie;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class PorteesController extends AbstractController
{
     // services are provided by the container (see Example 06)
     #[Route('/', name: 'portees', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function afficher(Request $request, CompteurService $compteur, RequeteInfos $infos,
        CookiesSignes $cookies): Response
    {
         // APPLICATION: the shared counter
        $total = $compteur->incrementer();
         // SESSION: browser-specific data, stored by SERVEUR
         // (a var/sessions file), retrieved via the session cookie
        $session = $request->getSession();
        $session->set('visites', $session->get('visites', 0) + 1);
         // CLIENT: data stored by NAVIGATEUR in cookies,
         // sent back to the server with each request; one in plain text, the other signed
        $mesVisites = (int) $request->cookies->get('mesVisites') + 1;
        $mesVisitesSigne = (int) $cookies->verifier($request->cookies->get('mesVisitesSigne')) + 1;
        $reponse = $this->render('portees/portees.html.twig', [
            'total' => $total, 'instance' => $infos->numero,
            'visitesSession' => $session->get('visites'), 'mesVisites' => $mesVisites,
            'mesVisitesSigne' => $mesVisitesSigne,
        ]);
        $reponse->headers->setCookie(Cookie::create('mesVisites', (string) $mesVisites));
        $reponse->headers->setCookie(Cookie::create('mesVisitesSigne', $cookies->signer((string) $mesVisitesSigne)));
        return $reponse;
    }
}
  • lines 19–20: the action receives the request and three services provided by the container;
  • line 23: the application scope;
  • lines 26–27: the session scope. [$request->getSession()] returns the user’s session; [get(cle, défaut)] reads a value, and [set(cle, valeur)] writes it. [Symfony] saves the session at the end of the request;
  • Lines 30–31: the client scope, with two cookies. Their values are strings provided by the browser and may therefore be missing or invalid: the conversion [(int)] returns 0 for [null] or for text that is not a number. The value of the signed cookie is accepted only if its signature is correct;
  • lines 32–39: To set a cookie, you need the response object: [render] constructs it (example 13), then [setCookie] adds the cookies to it. Without an expiration date, a cookie lasts until the browser is closed (this is a “session” cookie, as defined by browsers).

docs.text:
