docs.title: 6.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
After a few visits in a browser:

Let’s track the requests using [curl], which acts as a first browser by storing its cookies in the file [a.txt]:

curl -i -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:8000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
...
Set-Cookie: mesVisites=1; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: mesVisitesSigne=1.e50058404359cc9be2e65b8d9366aa98b7d7db4ca7ee576cfdffb6d1a1150d37; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=32da14307b05da3847ea54b2ae3e6f77; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...
      <li>application : 1 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
      <li>requête : objet n° 1 (n° 1 dans la vue),
        requête reçue à 09:48:29.888</li>
            <li>session : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (1 dans la vue)</li>
      <li>client : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (cookie en clair),
        1 (cookie signé)</li>
...

The response sets three cookies. The first, [mesVisites], contains the value in plain text. The second, [mesVisitesSigne], contains the same value, followed by a period and its signature. The third, [PHPSESSID], is the session ID. The session data is stored in a file on the server, [var/sessions/dev/sess_32da14307b05da3847ea54b2ae3e6f77], whose name matches the session ID:

_sf2_attributes|a:1:{s:7:"visites";i:1;}_sf2_meta|a:3:{s:1:"u";i:1790502509;s:1:"c";i:1790502509;s:1:"l";i:0;}

In the serialization format of [PHP], we can see an array with a single key, [visites], and an integer value of 1 ([i:1]), followed by information from [Symfony] regarding the session (creation and last use dates). A second visit, with the same cookies:

curl -i -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:8000/

...
Set-Cookie: mesVisites=2; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: mesVisitesSigne=2.4c7239f31c7e195c32dc5dcf2c7734ea05e6cb316eeab9a53239ab047db525ff; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...
      <li>application : 2 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
      <li>requête : objet n° 2 (n° 2 dans la vue),
        requête reçue à 09:48:32.813</li>
            <li>session : 2 visite(s) de ce navigateur (2 dans la vue)</li>
      <li>client : 2 visite(s) de ce navigateur (cookie en clair),
        2 (cookie signé)</li>
...

The session already exists: the [PHPSESSID] cookie is not sent back. A second “browser,” with its own cookie file, which is initially empty:

curl -c b.txt -b b.txt http://localhost:8000/

      <li>application : 3 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
      <li>requête : objet n° 3 (n° 3 dans la vue),
        requête reçue à 09:48:32.826</li>
            <li>session : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (1 dans la vue)</li>
      <li>client : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (cookie en clair),
        1 (cookie signé)</li>

The application counter has continued; the session and cookies for the second browser start over at 1. Each request had its own [RequeteInfos] object, and in each one, the action and view saw the same one. Finally, a malicious user forges their own cookies: 1,000 visits in [mesVisites], 999 in [mesVisitesSigne] (with a fabricated signature), and a session ID of their own invention:

curl -i -b "mesVisites=1000;mesVisitesSigne=999.abc;PHPSESSID=abc" http://localhost:8000/

...
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=1885ac965cf2dc862c4aecb994300956; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...
      <li>application : 4 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
      ...
            <li>session : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (1 dans la vue)</li>
      <li>client : 1001 visite(s) de ce navigateur (cookie en clair),
        1 (cookie signé)</li>

The plaintext cookie was accepted as is: 1,001 visits. The cookie [mesVisitesSigne], however, did not have the correct signature: it was ignored, as if it were missing. Copying the signature from another value (such as that of [1], next to the value [999]) doesn’t work any better: the signature depends on the value. As for the made-up session ID, it does not correspond to any existing session: [Symfony] rejects it (this is the “strict” mode for [PHP] sessions) and creates a new session with a new ID. The user therefore cannot choose another user’s session.

Let’s remember the rule: data coming from the client is trustworthy only if it is protected by the server (signed, as here or as with the token in the chapter on authentication, or encrypted); data that has nothing to hide, and whose value is verified by the server (the language in Example 22), can remain in plaintext. A signature guarantees that a value has not been altered, but it does not hide it: a secret must never be entrusted to the client, even if it is signed.

docs.title: 10. Interim Conclusion
docs.text:
Examples 01 through 28 have presented, one by one, all the concepts required by the case study:

controllers, actions, routing, responses, redirects01 through 05[config/routes.yaml], folder [src/Controller]service container, dependency injection06[config/services.yaml], all buildersaction model, binding, validation constraints07 through 12[src/Web/Outils.php] (raw parameter reading), [src/Metier/DonneesPersonne.php]views [Twig], template, fragments, macros, extensions13 to 16folder [templates], [src/Twig/VuesExtension.php]Form component forms, validation, redisplay17 to 19folder [src/Form], [templates/macros.html.twig]POST / Redirect / GET, flash messages, cache20[src/Web/Flash.php], [templates/fragments/succes.html.twig]links and buttons, CSRF protection, confirmation window21[src/Web/Controleur.php], [fragments/confirmation.html.twig], [public/js/app.js]internationalization22folder [translations], [src/EventListener/FixerLangue.php], [LangueController.php]data scope, cache, session, cookies23[src/Web/ApplicationModel.php] (cache), [src/Securite] (cache, cookies), sessionkernel events, listeners, error pages24folder [src/EventListener], [templates/erreur.html.twig]firewall, JWT authenticator, roles, CAPTCHA, rate limiting25 to 27[config/packages/security.yaml], folder [src/Securite], [AuthController.php]Web / business / DAO, [Doctrine], transactions28files [src/Entity], [src/Dao], [src/Metier]

The case study brings them together into a complete, realistic-sized application (about 100 files, approximately 7,000 lines, including comments). It was written with the same care as the examples: each file begins with a comment explaining its role, and tricky sections are annotated in the code. Each main folder also contains a file named [README.md] that lists its files. The document’s comments highlight what the examples did not show and refer to them for the rest.

docs.title: 5. Internationalization
docs.text:
An internationalized application displays its text in the user’s language. The case study is in French and English. The principle is simple: the views no longer contain text, but keys ([MENU.ACCUEIL]), and a dictionary for each language associates a text with each key. The selected language is stored in a cookie.

[Symfony] includes a translation component, the Translator, which we already encountered in Example 09 for validation messages. Its dictionaries are stored in the [translations] folder, with one file per domain and per language: [validators.fr.yaml] (the validation messages domain, Example 09), [messages.fr.yaml] (the default domain, the one for our texts). The YAML format allows for nested keys: this is how the dictionaries for versions [ASP.NET Core MVC], [NestJS], [Spring MVC], [Flask], and [Laravel] from the case study, with the exception of syntax. For the syntax of the messages themselves, we choose the ICU format (International Components for Unicode), a standard that the [intl] extension of [PHP] can interpret, and which, for example, can inflect text into the plural form. The formatting of dates and amounts remains the same as in Example 16.

docs.title: 5.1. Example 22: A Bilingual Application
docs.text:
22-i18n/
├── config/
│   └── packages/
│       └── framework.yaml
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   ├── LangueController.php
│   │   └── PagesController.php
│   ├── EventListener/
│   │   └── DefinirLangue.php
│   ├── Modele/
│   │   └── Produit.php
│   └── Twig/
│       └── FormatsExtension.php
├── templates/
│   ├── fragments/
│   │   └── navbar.html.twig
│   ├── layout.html.twig
│   └── pages/
│       ├── accueil.html.twig
│       └── produits.html.twig
├── translations/
│   ├── messages+intl-icu.en.yaml
│   └── messages+intl-icu.fr.yaml
└── ...

docs.title: 5.1.1. The configuration: config/packages/framework.yaml
docs.text:
# config/packages/framework.yaml: FrameworkBundle configuration
framework:
    secret: '%env(APP_SECRET)%'
     # the default language and the languages supported by the application
    default_locale: fr
    enabled_locales: ['fr', 'en']
     # the TRADUCTION service; its dictionaries are in the translations/ folder.
     # If a key is missing from the English dictionary, it is looked up in the French dictionary
    translator:
        default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/translations'
        fallbacks: ['fr']
  • Line 5: the application’s default language, which is used for requests that do not specify a language (Example 09);
  • line 6: the languages supported by the application. This list is used by [Symfony] (the profiler, localized route generation, etc.); our own code also has its own list, in the listener [DefinirLangue];
  • lines 9–11: the translation service. [fallbacks] specifies the fallback language(s): if a key is missing from the requested language’s dictionary, it is looked up in the French dictionary. A key missing from all dictionaries is displayed as-is: this way, any omission is immediately visible on the screen.

docs.title: 5.1.2. The Dictionaries
docs.text:
The file [translations/messages+intl-icu.fr.yaml]:

# translations/messages+intl-icu.fr.yaml: the French dictionary.
# messages: the default domain; +intl-icu: messages follow the ICU syntax
# ({name}: a parameter; {n, plural, ...}: a message that depends on a number)
MENU:
    ACCUEIL: Accueil
    PRODUITS: Produits
ACCUEIL:
    TITRE: Bienvenue
    BONJOUR: 'Bonjour {nom} !'
    DATE: 'Nous sommes le {date}.'
PRODUITS:
    TITRE: Nos produits
    NOM: Produit
    PRIX: Prix
    NOMBRE: '{n, plural, =0 {Aucun produit} one {# product} other {# products}} in the catalog.'

The file name consists of three parts: the domain ([messages], the default domain), the suffix [+intl-icu], which indicates messages in the ICU format, and the language ([fr]). Keys are grouped by topic using the YAML nesting structure: the menu item “Home” has the key [MENU.ACCUEIL], with levels separated by a period. A text may contain parameters, written as [{nom}], which are replaced during translation.

  • Line 9: Apostrophes delimit a string YAML; they are necessary when the text contains characters that YAML interprets (curly braces, colons, etc.);
  • Line 15: a plural message. [{n, plural, ...}] selects a form based on the value of the parameter [n]: [=0] for exactly 0, [one] for the singular, [other] for the plural; [#] is replaced by the number. Plural rules depend on the language, and ICU knows them: in French, 0 and 1 are singular, whereas in English, 0 is plural (“0 products”). This is an improvement over the “product(s)” used in previous versions of the case study.

The file [translations/messages+intl-icu.en.yaml] has exactly the same keys:

# translations/messages+intl-icu.en.yaml: the English dictionary; same keys
MENU:
    ACCUEIL: Home
    PRODUITS: Products
ACCUEIL:
    TITRE: Welcome
    BONJOUR: 'Hello {nom}!'
    DATE: 'Today is {date}.'
PRODUITS:
    TITRE: Our products
    NOM: Product
    PRIX: Price
    NOMBRE: '{n, plural, =0 {No products} one {# product} other {# products}} in the catalog.'

Without the suffix [+intl-icu], the parameters would be written as [%nom%], and the plural would use a syntax specific to [Symfony] ([{0} Aucun produit|{1} Un produit|]1, Inf[ %n% produits]). The format ICU is the one currently recommended by the [Symfony] documentation.

docs.title: 5.1.3. The language of each query: src/EventListener/DefinirLangue.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/EventListener/DefinirLangue.php: the language of each request

namespace App\EventListener;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\RequestEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;

// priority 20: after routing, before the Symfony listeners that use the language (see Example 16)
#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::REQUEST, priority: 20)]
class DefinirLangue
{
     // the supported languages; the first is the default language
    public const LANGUES = ['fr', 'en'];

    public const COOKIE = 'langue';

     // the language of the [langue] cookie, if supported; otherwise, French
    public function __invoke(RequestEvent $evenement): void
    {
        $requete = $evenement->getRequest();
        $langue = $requete->cookies->get(self::COOKIE);
        $requete->setLocale(in_array($langue, self::LANGUES, true) ? $langue : self::LANGUES[0]);
    }
}

This is the [FixerLangue] listener from Example 16, which this time retrieves the language from a cookie:

  • line 11: the [kernel.request] event listener, with priority 20: after routing, but before the [Symfony] listeners that use the request language (Example 16);
  • lines 15–17: the supported languages and the cookie name: public class constants, accessible from other classes ([DefinirLangue::LANGUES]);
  • lines 22–24: the request language: the language of the [langue] cookie if one exists and is supported; otherwise, French. [$requete->cookies] is the set of cookies sent by the browser (example 05); [get] returns the value of a cookie, or [null]. [in_array], with [true] as the third parameter, also compares the types ([===]). [setLocale] sets the request language: this is the language used by the translator, our formatting filters, and the [format_currency] filter of [Twig].

Unlike [Laravel], [Symfony] does not encrypt cookies: the [langue] cookie is transmitted in plain text. This is not a problem: it contains no confidential information, and the server accepts only supported languages. The following example revisits the issue of how much trust can be placed in a cookie.

docs.title: 5.1.4. Language selection: src/Controller/LangueController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/LangueController.php: the language selection

namespace App\Controller;

use App\EventListener\DefinirLangue;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Cookie;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class LangueController extends AbstractController
{
     // GET /language/en: saves the selection in a cookie, then returns to the previous page.
     // requirements: any language other than "fr" or "en" does not match the route (404)
     #[Route('/langue/{code}', name: 'langue', requirements: ['code' => 'fr|en'], methods: ['GET'])]
    public function changer(Request $request, string $code): RedirectResponse
    {
        $reponse = $this->redirect(self::pageDOrigine($request));
         // the cookie: valid for one year, unreadable by the JavaScript on the page (httpOnly),
         // never sent with a request from another site (POST) (sameSite lax)
        $reponse->headers->setCookie(Cookie::create(DefinirLangue::COOKIE, $code)
            ->withExpires(new \DateTimeImmutable('+1 year'))
            ->withHttpOnly(true)
            ->withSameSite(Cookie::SAMESITE_LAX));
        return $reponse;
    }

     // the page from which we came (Referer header), of which we retain only the path:
     // Redirecting to a full URL from the request would allow
     // to send the user to another site (“open redirect” vulnerability)
    private static function pageDOrigine(Request $request): string
    {
         // parse_url breaks down a URL into its components (path, parameters, etc.)
        $url = parse_url($request->headers->get('Referer', ''));
        $chemin = $url['path'] ?? '';
         // "//site.com/..." would be interpreted by the browser as a URL
         // on a AUTRE site: also rejected
        if (! str_starts_with($chemin, '/') || str_starts_with($chemin, '//')) {
            return '/';
        }
        return isset($url['query']) ? "$chemin?{$url['query']}" : $chemin;
    }
}
  • line 17: the route [/langue/{code}]. The option [requirements] (example 02) limits the parameter to the two supported languages: [/langue/de] does not correspond to any route and returns a 404 error;
  • line 20: the action responds with a redirect to the page the user came from: the user is taken back to their page in the new language;
  • Lines 23–26: The response contains a cookie, which the browser will send back with every request. The [Cookie] class of [Symfony] describes it: [Cookie::create(nom, valeur)] creates it, and each method of [with...] returns a modified copy (an immutable object; see Example 03): [withExpires], the expiration date (in one year); [withHttpOnly(true)] makes it invisible to the [JavaScript] on the page; [withSameSite(Cookie::SAMESITE_LAX)] prevents the browser from sending it with a POST request from another site. ([httpOnly] and [lax] are, incidentally, the default values for [Cookie::create].) [$reponse->headers->setCookie] adds it to the response as a [Set-Cookie] header;
  • lines 33–44: the original page is specified by the [Referer] header in the request (the misspelled version, with a single [r], is the one used in the HTTP standard), which the browser populates with the URL from the page that contained the link. But this header comes from the client, which can put anything in it. Blindly redirecting to this address would turn our application into an open redirect: a malicious link bearing our domain name could send the user to a malicious site. Therefore, we retain only the path and parameters from URL (the [parse_url] function from [PHP] breaks it down into its components in an associative array), and we reject any path that begins with [//], which the browser would interpret as the address of another site.

docs.title: 5.1.5. Actions: src/Controller/PagesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/PagesController.php: the actions are not language-aware:
// they provide data, and the views translate and format it

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Modele\Produit;
use DateTimeImmutable;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

#[Route(methods: ['GET'])]
class PagesController extends AbstractController
{
     #[Route('/', name: 'accueil')]
    public function accueil(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('pages/accueil.html.twig', ['nom' => 'Marie',
            'aujourdhui' => new DateTimeImmutable('2026-09-23')]);
    }

     #[Route('/produits', name: 'produits')]
    public function produits(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('pages/produits.html.twig', ['produits' => [
            new Produit('Clavier', 2500),
            new Produit('Souris', 1250),
            new Produit('Écran', 114900),
        ]]);
    }
}

The actions are language-agnostic: they provide raw data (a name, a date, amounts in cents). Translation and formatting are handled by the views. The class [Produit] has a name and a price in cents; the extension [FormatsExtension] is the one from Example 16: its filter [date_longue] writes a date in the “full” format of the query language (“Wednesday, September 23, 2026,” “Wednesday, September 23, 2026”), and its filter [monnaie] writes an amount.

docs.title: 5.1.6. Translate in the views
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{# app.request.locale: the language of the request, "fr" or "en" #}
<html lang="{{ app.request.locale }}">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  {# title: the [titre] block of the page, already translated #}
  <title>{% block titre %}{% endblock %}</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ path('bootstrap', {fichier: 'css/bootstrap.min.css'}) }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ asset('css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    {% include 'fragments/navbar.html.twig' %}
    <main>
      {% block contenu %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • line 3: the page’s [lang] attribute indicates its language to browsers, search engines, and screen readers; [app.request.locale] is the query language;
  • line 8: the page title is provided by the page itself, already translated (block [titre]).
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <div class="navbar-nav me-auto">
    {# 'CLE'|trans: the translation of a key, in the request language #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{{ path('accueil') }}">{{ 'MENU.ACCUEIL'|trans }}</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="{{ path('produits') }}">{{ 'MENU.PRODUITS'|trans }}</a>
  </div>
  {# the current language is highlighted #}
  <div class="btn-group btn-group-sm">
    {% for code in ['fr', 'en'] %}
      <a class="btn {{ app.request.locale == code ? 'btn-primary' : 'btn-outline-primary' }}"
         href="{{ path('langue', {code: code}) }}">{{ code|upper }}</a>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
</nav>
  • lines 4–5: the filter [trans] translates a key into the language of the request;
  • lines 9–12: one button per language, which triggers the action [/langue/{code}]. The current language is highlighted ([btn-primary], solid button).
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}
{% block titre %}{{ 'ACCUEIL.TITRE'|trans }}{% endblock %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1>{{ 'ACCUEIL.TITRE'|trans }}</h1>
  {# a parameter: the trans filter parameter, an associative array #}
  <p>{{ 'ACCUEIL.BONJOUR'|trans({nom: nom}) }}</p>
  {# the date, first formatted (filter date_longue, see Example 16), then passed as a parameter [date] #}
  <p>{{ 'ACCUEIL.DATE'|trans({date: aujourdhui|date_longue}) }}</p>
{% endblock %}
  • line 2: the translated [titre] block for the template;
  • line 7: the parameters for a text are provided in an associative array, a parameter of the [trans] filter; [{nom}] is replaced by the value of the key [nom];
  • line 9: the date, formatted in the query language by the [date_longue] filter, then passed as a parameter.
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}
{% block titre %}{{ 'PRODUITS.TITRE'|trans }}{% endblock %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1>{{ 'PRODUITS.TITRE'|trans }}</h1>
  <table class="table table-sm w-auto">
    <thead><tr><th>{{ 'PRODUITS.NOM'|trans }}</th><th class="text-end">{{ 'PRODUITS.PRIX'|trans }}</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for produit in produits %}
        <tr>
          <td>{{ produit.nom }}</td>
          {# the currency filter from Example 16: the format depends on the language #}
          <td class="text-end">{{ produit.prixCentimes|monnaie }}</td>
        </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
  {# the message in the plural form: ICU selects the form based on parameter n #}
  <p>{{ 'PRODUITS.NOMBRE'|trans({n: produits|length}) }}</p>
{% endblock %}
  • line 13: the filter [monnaie], whose result depends on the language;
  • line 19: the [n] parameter for the plural form of the message: the number of products ([length], example 14). The product names themselves are not translated: they are data that, in a real application, would come from a database.

Outside of views, the translator is a service of type [TranslatorInterface], which an action or service can receive via injection: [$traducteur->trans('ACCUEIL.BONJOUR', ['nom' => 'Marie'])].

docs.title: 5.1.7. Execution
docs.text:
The home page, in French (the default language), then in English after clicking the "EN" button:

The products page, in both languages. The amounts follow the conventions of each language:

The language switch, as seen with [curl]. The option [-H] provides the header [Referer] that the browser would send:

curl -i -H "Referer: http://localhost:8000/produits" http://localhost:8000/language/en

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
...
Location: /produits
...
Set-Cookie: langue=en; expires=Mon, 27 Sep 2027 09:47:37 GMT; Max-Age=31536000; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax

The redirect takes you back to the original page ([Symfony] writes a relative URL, which the browser completes), and the cookie is set for one year. A [Referer] that points to another site does not redirect you there: only its path is retained.

curl -i -H "Referer: https://pirate.example/piege" http://localhost:8000/language/en
curl -i -H "Referer: http://localhost:8000//pirate.example/x" http://localhost:8000/language/fr

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /piege
...
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /
...

The page [/piege] does not exist on our site: the user will receive a 404 error, but will remain on our site. Finally, the home page, requested with the cookie [langue=en] (option [-b] of [curl]):

curl -b "langue=en" http://localhost:8000/

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Welcome</title>
...
        <a class="nav-link" href="/">Home</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/produits">Products</a>
...
    <p>Hello Marie!</p>
    <p>Today is Wednesday, September 23, 2026.</p>
...

Another way to choose the language would have been to read the browser’s [Accept-Language] header (example 12; [$request->getPreferredLanguage(['fr', 'en'])] selects the best language from among those supported). The two are often combined: the browser’s language on the first visit, followed by the language the user has selected. A third method, commonly used with [Symfony], places the language in the URL ([/en/produits]): a special route parameter, [{_locale}], then sets the request language itself. This case study focuses on the cookie, with French as the default.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It follows the document “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Laravel] Web Framework” (2026), which itself followed the documents “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Flask] Web Framework,” "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Spring MVC] Web Framework," "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [ASP.NET Core MVC] Web Framework," and "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [NestJS] Web Framework" (2026). This document remains within the [PHP] universe but changes frameworks:

  • the [Laravel] framework is replaced by the [Symfony] 8.1 framework, still using the [PHP] language (version 8.4 or later);
  • the [Blade] views are replaced by [Twig] views, the view engine for [Symfony];
  • Validation using the rules in [Laravel] and form queries ([FormRequest]) is replaced by the Validator component in [Symfony] (constraints, written as [PHP] attributes) and by its Form component, which describes forms using classes;
  • the guards, middleware, and [Gate] components of [Laravel] are replaced by the Security component of [Symfony]: firewalls, authenticators, roles, password hashing, and an attempt limiter, supplemented by the [firebase/php-jwt] library for JWT tokens;
  • Middleware components, however, do not exist in [Symfony]: event listeners are used to intervene in request processing;
  • ORM [Eloquent] is replaced by [Doctrine], ORM is based on [Symfony], which in turn is based on [MySQL].

The document closely follows the structure of the [Laravel] course: first, numerous small projects, each focused on a single concept, followed by a comprehensive case study—a web application for scheduling appointments at a medical practice—with all files fully commented. The examples have the same numbers and cover the same topics as in courses [Laravel], [Flask], [Spring MVC], and [ASP.NET Core MVC]: A reader familiar with one of these courses can compare the frameworks on a case-by-case basis. However, this is not necessary: this document stands on its own and assumes no prior knowledge of these frameworks. The only prerequisites are a basic understanding of web programming (the HTTP protocol, the HTML language) and the fundamentals of the [PHP] language (variables, arrays, functions, classes). The course “Introduction to the PHP7 Language Through Examples” (2019) introduces the language itself for those who need to learn it first; the new features of [PHP] 8 used here (promoted properties, [readonly] classes, attributes, enumerations, named arguments, the null-safe operator, etc.) are explained when they first appear.

docs.title: 1.1. Symfony’s Role in a Web Application
docs.text:
A web application is often built in layers, with each layer communicating only with its neighboring layers:

  • the web layer receives requests HTTP from the browser and returns pages HTML to it. This is the layer that [Symfony] helps us write;
  • the business layer contains the application’s business rules (e.g., “a patient can have only one upcoming appointment”). It knows nothing about the web: it could just as easily serve a command-line application;
  • the data access layer (DAO layer, for Data Access Object) reads from and writes to the database. We will use [Doctrine], the ORM (Object Relational Mapper) associated with [Symfony], which maps table rows to [PHP] objects.

The web layer itself follows the MVC (Model-View-Controller) pattern:

  • the controller (C) is a class [PHP] whose methods, called actions, each handle a specific type of request (for example, [GET /agenda]). An action reads the request parameters, processes the request through the business layer, and then selects the view to display;
  • the model (M) is the set of data that the action passes to the view;
  • the view (V) is a [Twig] file (extension [.html.twig]): a HTML page that contains [{{ ... }}] expressions and [{% if %}], [{% for %}]... instructions, which the [Twig] engine replaces with data from the template.

A note on terminology, to avoid confusion: in [Symfony], the classes that represent database tables are called entities (document [src/Entity]). In this document, the term “model” will therefore always refer to the view model (the data passed to a view) or, in Chapter 2, the action model (the data it receives). The term “template” refers to the common view from which other pages inherit (chapter on views).

The processing of a request follows the numbered steps in the diagram:

  • 1: The browser sends a request, such as HTTP or [GET /agenda?idMedecin=1&jour=2026-09-26];
  • 2: The web server receives the request and passes it to the [Symfony] application via the [public/index.php] file. During development, this server is the one that includes [PHP], launched by the command [php -S localhost:8000 -t public]; in production, it will be a server such as [nginx] or [Apache], associated with [PHP-FPM]. The file [public/index.php] passes the request to the application’s kernel (kernel), which routes it through a series of events: classes from [Symfony] and the application, as well as listeners (session, security, language, etc.), are involved. One of them compares the requested path to the application’s routes and selects the action responsible for this request: this is routing;
  • 3: The action requests the data it needs from the business layer; if necessary, the business layer contacts the DAO layer, which queries the [MySQL] database in SQL;
  • 4: The action constructs the view’s M model and instructs the [Twig] engine to generate the page (method [render]);
  • 5: The page HTML generated by the view is the action’s response, which [Symfony] returns to the browser.

[Symfony] is, along with [Laravel], one of the two major web frameworks in the [PHP] world. Free and open-source, created in 2005 by Fabien Potencier (and the French company SensioLabs), it works anywhere that [PHP] ([Windows], [Linux], [macOS]), and [PHP] works with almost all web hosting providers. [Symfony] is primarily a collection of about fifty components—independent libraries (HTTP requests and responses, routing, the console, forms, validation, security, etc.)— so well-regarded that other projects use them: [Laravel] itself is built on several of them, and readers of the previous lesson have already encountered them. The [Symfony] framework assembles these components using bundles (integration packages) and a service container that creates the application’s objects. Compared to [Laravel], [Symfony] makes clear choices: no facades or global functions, but services obtained through dependency injection; explicit configuration in YAML files; [PHP] attributes ([#[Route]], [#[Assert\NotBlank]]...) to describe the code; a ORM and [Doctrine], which separate objects from their registration. It is a framework renowned for its rigor, its documentation, and its versioning policy: a minor release every six months, a “long-term support” release every two years, and the guarantee that an application without an obsolescence warning will transition to the next major version without modification. [Symfony] can create servers that return JSON to a [JavaScript] client ([Angular], [React], [Vue.js], [Flutter]...) as well as traditional web applications, where the server generates the HTML pages and the browser simply displays them. It is this second use case that this document examines.

A specific feature of [PHP] explains a great deal about [Symfony]: the application is rebuilt with each request and then discarded (example 01). [Symfony] offsets this cost by compiling its configuration once and for all into [PHP] code, which is stored in a cache ([var/cache] folder). We will return to this frequently.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • [PHP] 8.4 (any version 8.4 or later is suitable), with the extensions [intl], [mbstring], [openssl], and [pdo_mysql];
  • [Composer] 2, the library manager for [PHP];
  • the editor [Visual Studio Code], with the extensions [PHP Intelephense] (code analysis), [Twig Language 2] (views), and [YAML] (configuration files);
  • a modern browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]);
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays the raw HTTP responses (it is included with [Windows] 10 and 11);
  • SGBD, [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, that of [Laragon] under [Windows], starting with the chapter on data access, and for the case study. Under [Windows], [Laragon] installs [PHP], [Composer], and [MySQL] all at once.

[Symfony] and the other libraries are not part of [PHP]: [Composer] downloads them from the [Packagist] repository during installation (so you must be connected to the Internet on that day) and places them in a [vendor] folder. Each project describes its libraries in a [composer.json] file. The following table lists the main ones, along with the versions used:

[symfony/framework-bundle]the framework: core, routing, controllers, service container, configuration, session, cache; it installs the components it needs ([symfony/http-foundation], [symfony/http-kernel], [symfony/routing], [symfony/dependency-injection]...)8.1.7[symfony/twig-bundle], [twig/twig]the views [Twig] (chapter on views)8.1.7, 3.30.0[symfony/validator], [symfony/form]Validation (starting with Example 08) and forms (starting with Example 17)8.1.7[symfony/security-bundle]Authentication and Authorization (Security Chapter)8.1.7[symfony/translation]Translations (examples 09 and 22)8.1.7[doctrine/orm], [doctrine/dbal], [doctrine/doctrine-bundle]database access (example 28 and case study)3.7.2, 4.5.0, 3.3.2[firebase/php-jwt]tokens JWT (chapter on authentication)7.2.0

[Symfony] is typically installed by creating a complete project using the command:

composer create-project symfony/skeleton mon-projet

or using the [Symfony] command-line tool (the [symfony] program; see appendices): [symfony new mon-projet --webapp]. [Composer] then downloads the skeleton of a [Symfony] application, followed by its libraries. The skeleton also contains [Symfony Flex], a plugin for [Composer] that, each time a library ([composer require twig]) is installed, writes its own configuration files based on templates published online. This is how you start a real project. For learning purposes, this method has a drawback: the files appear on their own, without you knowing what they’re for. The examples in this document therefore start from the other end: Example 01 is the smallest possible [Symfony] application, and each example adds only the files it needs, written and commented on by hand. The case study at the end follows the structure of a standard [Symfony] application.

docs.title: 1.3.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
The case study requires SGBD, MySQL, a PHP interpreter, and the PHP and [composer] package installer. Laragon can provide all of this and more. As of September 2026, Laragon is available at URL and [Download Laragon – Fast & Modern Dev Environment ]. Laragon comes with tools that allow you to install a PHP server and the SGBD and [MySQL]:

  • in [1], an Apache web server;
  • in [2], the SGBD and [MySQL];
  • on [3], a messaging tool that we will not use;
  • [4] starts all services (Apache, [MySQL], MailPit);
  • [5] displays the web page for URL and [http://localhost]. By default, this URL refers to the <laragon-install>\www folder, where <laragon-install> is the Laragon installation folder;
  • in [6], launches the HeidiSQL tool, which allows you to manage MySQL databases. We will use this tool to create the database used by the tax calculation server;
  • In [7], open a terminal; all the binaries needed for Laragon are located in PATH;
  • In [8], open a Windows Explorer window in the folder associated with URL and [http://localhost];

The Laragon installation folder contains the following items:

  • In [1], the [bin] folder contains numerous applications:
  • In [1], the Apache web server;
  • in [2], a command-line terminal;
  • in [3], a [git] client that allows you to manage different versions of a project;
  • in [4], a database manager;
  • in [5], a mail manager;
  • in [6], the SGBD and [MySQL];
  • [7], another web server;
  • in [8], [node.js] to run JavaScript scripts;
  • [9], a text editor;
  • [10], the PHP interpreter;
  • [11], the [Python] interpreter;
  • [12], a cache server;

Laragon comes with a comprehensive development environment. In this course, we will use:

  • SGBD, [MySQL], [6], and the [heidisql] tool for graphical management;
  • the PHP 8.5 interpreter;
  • the [composer] package installer;

The README from the case study indicates that you must enter the following commands in a terminal:

composer install

to install the PHP packages required for the examples and the case study.

php -S localhost:8000 -t public

to run either one of the examples or the case study. If you use a [PowerShell] terminal within VSCode, you will encounter the following problem: Neither [composer] nor [php] are present in the PATH directory on the Windows machine after installing Laragon. Therefore, these commands will not be recognized in a VSCode terminal.

To include [composer] and [php] in the PATH on the Windows machine, open a PowerShell terminal in [administrateur] mode, then type the following commands:


[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path",[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine") + ";C:\laragon\bin\composer","Machine")


[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path",[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine") + ";C:\laragon\bin\php\php-8.5.11-nts-Win32-vs17-x64","Machine")

Adjust the two highlighted paths to match your environment.

You will need to restart VSCode for these changes to take effect.

To create the [MySQL] database required for the case study, proceed as follows:

  • In [1], all services must be started;
  • in [2], the [Database] option allows you to manage the database;

The [Database] option launches a utility called HeidiSQL:

  • In [1], you can select various SGBD options. The default value provided is SGBD MySQL. This is acceptable;
  • in [2], you log in to HeidiSQL;
  • In [1-2], run the SQL file, then select the [dbrdvmedecins2.sql] file, which you’ll find in the [symfony-sept-202-] folder:

Running the [3] file will create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database used by the case study. To view it, run F5 within HeidiSQL to refresh the display:

Editor's note: The following screenshots show a database named [dbrdvmedecins], whereas the database in the case study is named [dbrdvmedecins2]. The two databases are virtually identical, so we determined that it was unnecessary to take new screenshots.

End of note

The database [dbrdvmedecins] has been created. Here is its content:

  • in [1-3], the table [clients];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the row’s version number. This number increments each time the row is modified;
    • [titre, nom, prenom] identifies the person;

  • in [1-3], the table [medecins];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the version number of the row;
    • [titre, nom, prenom] identifies the person;

  • In [1-3], the table of doctors’ appointment time slots:
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: row version number;
    • [id-medecin]: foreign key referencing the doctor’s primary key;
    • [hdebut, mdebut]: hour and minutes of the appointment start time. Thus, [8,20] means 8:20 a.m.
    • [hfin, mfin]: hour and minutes of the end of the consultation.

  • In [1-3], the [rv] table of scheduled appointments;
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: version number;
    • [jour]: appointment date;
    • [id_creneau]: foreign key referencing the primary key of the appointment time slot. Since a time slot is linked to a doctor, we know which doctor is handling this appointment;
    • [id_client]: foreign key to the number (primary key) of the patient attending the appointment;

  • in [1-3], the table [users] lists the users authorized to use the application [NestJS];
    • [id, version]: primary key, version number;
    • [login, password]: user credentials;
    • [nom]: user name;
    • [role]: the user’s role. [ADMIN] has full access rights. [USER] has read-only access. This user can view a doctor’s schedule but cannot schedule or cancel an appointment;

docs.title: 1.3.2. Running the Case Study
docs.text:
Reviewer’s note: I advise the reader to run the case study immediately as described below. Once you fully understand the purpose of this appointment scheduling application, ask your favorite IA to modify the application as follows: from now on, each doctor will be able to:

  • set their own appointment slots between two dates. This will allow them to adjust their schedule as needed;
  • remove certain time slots from the calendar for a given day—for example, if they are unavailable for personal reasons;

The modification is not straightforward because it involves a change to the database structure. Ask IA to provide you with the new application code and the SQL script to create the new database. To do this, you’ll need to provide them with the ZIP file containing the complete project as well as the SQL script for the old database.

Also, I haven’t reviewed the course created by Claude. He had already produced the courses [NestJS], [ASP.NET Core MVC], [Spring MVC], and [Flask], all of which were perfect. I assumed the same was true for this one. If you run into a problem understanding something, the solution is always the same: ask your favorite IA to explain what you don’t understand. Claude, for example, is very good at this. You may need to “upload” the example you don’t understand to him.

End of note.

The case study at the end of this document is a complete application. Readers will likely want to see it in action before delving into the details of the framework: here’s how to run it. It is located in the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder, next to the [exemples] folder:

symfony-sept-2026/
├── exemples/
└── rdvmedecins2-symfony/

You must have installed [PHP] (version 8.4 or later), [Composer], [Visual Studio Code], and [MySQL] (see appendices). Then:

  • Create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database by running the [rdvmedecins2-symfony/database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. Using [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu. At the command line, from the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder:
mysql -u root < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
  • Open the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder in [Visual Studio Code] (File menu / Open Folder), then open a terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal);
  • Install the application libraries: [Composer] reads the file [composer.json], downloads [Symfony] and the other libraries, and places them in the application’s [vendor] folder (takes a few tens of seconds):
composer install
  • Check the connection to the database. The application connects to [MySQL] on [127.0.0.1], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password (the default settings for [Laragon]). If your [root] account has a password, enter it in the application’s [.env] file, on the line [DATABASE_URL]: [mysql://root:monMotDePasse@127.0.0.1:3306/dbrdvmedecins2...];
  • Run the application:
php -S localhost:8081 -t public
  • [PHP] displays:
[Sun Sep 27 18:40:12 2026] PHP 8.4.21 Development Server (http://(localhost:8081) started

The development server is listening on port 8081 on the machine ([localhost]). Each request received will be logged in the console, along with messages from [Symfony] (the selected route, the SQL commands sent to the database);

  • Open the address [http://localhost:8081] in a browser:

  • Log in with one of the demo accounts, whose password is the same as the username: [admin] (administrator), [pelissier], [tatou], [dupont] (doctors), [martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german] (patients). You must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase.

An application with the ID [PHP] fails to read the database upon startup: a connection error only appears on the first page that queries the database, i.e., at the time of connection. [Symfony] then displays its detailed error page and logs the error to the server console. If the message is [SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] Connection refused], it means that [MySQL] has not started; with [[1045] Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'], it means the password is incorrect; with [[1049] Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2'], it means the script SQL was not executed; with [could not find driver], that the [pdo_mysql] extension of [PHP] is not enabled. If the page displays [Failed opening required '.../vendor/autoload_runtime.php'], it means that [composer install] was not executed; if the [php -S] command fails with the message [Failed to listen on localhost:8081 (reason: Address already in use)], it means that port 8081 is already in use (by another version of the application, for example). The application’s [README.md] file describes other scenarios. Stop the application using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal.

The case study at the end of the document demonstrates how to use the application and then explains each of its files.

docs.title: 1.4. Examples
docs.text:
The examples are stored in the [exemples] folder, with one subfolder per example:

exemples/
├── 01-structure/
├── 02-routage/
├── ...
├── 28-couches/
├── commun/
│   ├── bootstrap/
│   ├── BootstrapController.php
│   └── README.md
└── composer.json

Each example is a small application ([Symfony]) that runs on its own. All examples use the same libraries, described in the file [exemples/composer.json]:

{
    "name": "cours/symfony-exemples",
    "description": "Les 28 exemples du cours [Introduction étape par étape au framework web Symfony] : un seul dossier vendor, partagé par tous les exemples",
    "type": "project",
    "license": "MIT",
    "require": {
        "php": ">=8.4",
        "ext-intl": "*",
        "ext-pdo_mysql": "*",
        "doctrine/doctrine-bundle": "^3.3",
        "doctrine/orm": "^3.7",
        "firebase/php-jwt": "^7.2",
        "symfony/asset": "^8.1",
        "symfony/console": "^8.1",
        "symfony/dotenv": "^8.1",
        "symfony/form": "^8.1",
        "symfony/framework-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/intl": "^8.1",
        "symfony/lock": "^8.1",
        "symfony/rate-limiter": "^8.1",
        "symfony/security-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/serializer": "^8.1",
        "symfony/translation": "^8.1",
        "symfony/twig-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/validator": "^8.1",
        "symfony/yaml": "^8.1",
        "twig/intl-extra": "^3.30",
        "twig/twig": "^3.30"
    },
    "autoload": {
        "psr-4": {
            "Commun\\": "commun/"
        }
    },
    "config": {
        "optimize-autoloader": true,
        "sort-packages": true
    },
    "minimum-stability": "stable",
    "prefer-stable": true
}
  • Lines 6–29: What the examples require: [PHP] 8.4 or later, the extensions [intl] (language-specific formatting of numbers and dates, Example 16) and [pdo_mysql] (access to [MySQL], example 28), followed by the libraries, in alphabetical order: [Doctrine] (example 28), [firebase/php-jwt] (the tokens in JWT, example 25), and the components and bundles in [Symfony] that the examples use. [^8.1] reads “version 8.1, or a version newer than major version 8”;
  • lines 30–34: the classes in the [Commun] namespace are located in the [commun] folder (the PSR-4 rule, shown in Example 01): this is the shared controller that serves [Bootstrap] (Example 15);
  • the other lines configure the behavior of [Composer]: the class loader is optimized, libraries are sorted by name, and only stable versions are accepted.

To run the examples, first install their libraries—once and for all—in a terminal window open to the [exemples] folder:

composer install

[Composer] creates the [exemples/vendor] folder, shared by all 28 examples, and the [composer.lock] file, which records the exact versions installed (see case study). The [commun] folder contains the CSS framework, [Bootstrap] ([commun/bootstrap])—shared by the examples that format their pages (starting with Example 15)—and the controller that serves it ([commun/BootstrapController.php]; see Example 15).

Almost all of the examples have the same structure—that of a standard [Symfony] application, stripped down to the essentials. For example, the one in Example 13:

13-premiere-vue/
├── bin/
│   └── console
├── config/
│   ├── packages/
│   │   ├── framework.yaml
│   │   └── twig.yaml
│   ├── bundles.php
│   ├── routes.yaml
│   └── services.yaml
├── public/
│   └── index.php
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   └── VuesController.php
│   ├── Modele/
│   │   └── PageModele.php
│   └── Kernel.php

│   └── vues/
│       ├── inconnu.html.twig
│       └── index.html.twig

  • [public/index.php]: the entry point for all requests; [src/Kernel.php]: the application core; [bin/console]: the command-line tool for [Symfony] (Example 01);
  • [config]: configuration: application bundles ([bundles.php]), the configuration for each (folder [packages]), routes ([routes.yaml], Example 02), services ([services.yaml], Example 06);
  • [src]: the application’s classes: controllers ([src/Controller]), models, services, etc.;
  • [templates]: the views [Twig] (starting with the chapter on views);
  • [.env]: settings specific to the example (Example 01); [var]: files that [Symfony] writes itself (the cache, the session).

To run an example, open a terminal in its folder (in [Visual Studio Code]: right-click the example folder, then select “Open in Integrated Terminal”), and type:

php -S localhost:8000 -t public

All examples listen on port 8000: you can only run one at a time (or you must change the port: [php -S localhost:8001 -t public]). Stop the server using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal. It is not necessary to restart the server after modifying a [PHP] file, a view, or the configuration: the changes take effect with the next request (example 01).

When you open the [exemples] folder within [Visual Studio Code], the [PHP Intelephense] extension analyzes all files, including those from [Symfony] in the [vendor] folder: In each file, you can take advantage of code completion, navigation to the definition of a class or method ([F12] key), and error reporting. Since all examples have their classes in the [App] namespace, the extension may flag “duplicate” classes: this has no effect on execution, since each example runs independently. To avoid these warnings, simply open the example’s folder itself.

Each example introduces only a few new concepts, and the chapters build on one another: it is best to read them in order. The appendices describe how to install the tools: [PHP], [Composer], [Visual Studio Code] and its extensions, [MySQL] along with [Laragon], [curl], and the [symfony] tool.

docs.title: 9. Layered Architecture and Data Access
docs.text:
The previous examples stored their data in memory or in the cache. A real application stores it in a database and is organized into layers (see the diagram in the introduction):

  • the web layer (controllers, forms, views): read the request, call the business layer, select the view;
  • the business layer: business rules;
  • the DAO layer (Data Access Object): database queries.

Each layer is aware only of the layer below it, and as few of its details as possible: the web layer is unaware of SQL, and the business layer is unaware of HTML. This separation makes each layer easier to understand, test, and evolve. Example 28 applies this to managing a list of people: it is, on a smaller scale, the management of doctors and clients from the case study.

In [PHP], database access is organized across several layers:

  • The PDO extension (PHP Data Objects) of [PHP] defines a common interface for all SGBD extensions: open a connection, execute a SQL command, and read rows. Each SGBD has its own driver: [pdo_mysql] for [MySQL] (and [MariaDB]), included with [PHP];
  • The DBAL framework (Database Abstraction Layer) adds connection and transaction management, a query builder, type conversion, and translates errors from each SGBD into common exceptions (a uniqueness constraint violation becomes a [UniqueConstraintViolationException], regardless of the SGBD);
  • Doctrine ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) maps classes (entities) to database tables and transforms the retrieved rows into objects. It follows the so-called Data Mapper model: entities are ordinary objects that know nothing about the database; a separate object, the entity manager, reads and saves them. This is the difference between [Eloquent] and ORM (which is derived from [Laravel]), which follows the Active Record model (each object knows how to read and save itself, [$personne->save()]).

[Doctrine] does not belong to [Symfony]: it is an independent project, but ORM is the one recommended by [Symfony], and DoctrineBundle integrates it into the application. It is the equivalent of [JDBC], [JPA], and [Hibernate] in [Java] (which [Doctrine] was based on), [Entity Framework Core] into [C#], or [SQLAlchemy] into [Python]. Note a consequence of how [PHP] works: since nothing survives the request, each request opens its own connection to the database (upon its first request, SQL) and closes it upon termination. There is no connection pool as in [Java] or [Python]; opening a connection to [MySQL] on the same machine takes only a fraction of a millisecond.

The example requires a running [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]) server: the appendix explains how to install one using [Laragon].

docs.title: 9.1. Example 28: A Three-Tier Personnel Management System
docs.text:
28-couches/
├── .env
├── config/
