docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The [dbpersonnes] database is created by the SQL script. Using [Laragon], you can run it, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line, from the example folder:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersonnes.sql

The [database/dbpersonnes.sql] file:

-- Example 28 database: a single table, [personnes]
-- The script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersonnes;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersonnes CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersonnes;

CREATE TABLE personnes (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
   -- the row version, incremented with each modification (see layer DAO)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  prenom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  nom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
   -- No two people can have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_personnes_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO personnes (prenom, nom, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The script is written in [UTF-8]; this is specified to the server so that the accents in the data ([Pélissier]) remain intact;
  • Line 5: The character set [utf8mb4] accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] collation compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents: for [MySQL], [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 11: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 17: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names.

[Doctrine] can also create the tables itself, based on entities (command [bin/console doctrine:schema:create]), or through migrations: [PHP] classes that describe, step by step, the creation and modification of each table (library [DoctrineMigrationsBundle], command [bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate]). We maintain a script, SQL, which is common to all versions of the case study and shows exactly what the database contains.

docs.title: 9.1.2. Configuration
docs.text:
DoctrineBundle is added to the list of bundles:

<?php
// config/bundles.php: the application bundles; DoctrineBundle includes
// Doctrine (DBAL and ORM), the database access library
return [
    Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\FrameworkBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Symfony\Bundle\TwigBundle\TwigBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Doctrine\Bundle\DoctrineBundle\DoctrineBundle::class => ['all' => true],
];

The connection to the database is described in the file [.env] by a URL:

# .env: the configuration for Example 28 (see Example 01)
APP_ENV=dev
APP_SECRET=fe7d5dd3bafdb5b7ffcab097dd4e1c0c
# the database connection: SGBD MySQL, on this machine (127.0.0.1), port 3306,
# the `dbpersonnes` database, the `root` user without a password (Laragon settings)
DATABASE_URL="mysql://root:@127.0.0.1:3306/dbpersonnes?serverVersion=8.0.32&charset=utf8mb4"

The URL [DATABASE_URL] combines all the connection parameters: the SGBD ([mysql]), the username and password ([root], with nothing following [:]), the host and port, and finally the database name. If your server has a password, enter it after [:] ([root:secret@...]). Two parameters follow [?]: [serverVersion], the server version ([Doctrine] adapts the SQL it generates for each version; for [MariaDB], for example, we would write [serverVersion=10.11.2-MariaDB]), and [charset], the character set used for communication with the server, which is the database’s character set. The configuration of DoctrineBundle:

# config/packages/doctrine.yaml: the configuration for DoctrineBundle
doctrine:
     # DBAL: the database connection, described by a URL (.env file)
    dbal:
        url: '%env(resolve:DATABASE_URL)%'
         # SQL commands are written to the log (console) in debug mode
        logging: '%kernel.debug%'
     # ORM: the ENTITÉS, the classes associated with the tables, are the classes in the
     # src/Entity; their correspondence with the tables is described by PHP attributes
    orm:
        mappings:
            App:
                type: attribute
                dir: '%kernel.project_dir%/src/Entity'
                prefix: 'App\Entity'
  • line 5: the connection. The prefix [resolve:] replaces any references to other parameters ([%...%]) in the variable’s value, if present;
  • line 7: In debug mode, each SQL command is written to the log, which we can view in the console (Example 24). This is also the default setting;
  • lines 10–15: The entities are the classes in the [src/Entity] folder, whose namespace begins with [App\Entity]; their mapping to the tables is described by [PHP] attributes.

The other configuration files are those from Example 21: the session, anti-CSRF protection, and the methods PUT and DELETE ([framework.yaml]), as well as the form theme [Bootstrap] ([twig.yaml]). There is nothing else to configure: the classes for the three layers are created by the [Symfony] container, which injects the layer below into each one (the controller receives the business layer, the business layer receives the DAO layer), and DoctrineBundle registers the entity manager ([EntityManagerInterface]) with the container.

docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person entity
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Personne.php: a row in the table [personnes], a Doctrine ENTITÉ

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

// #[ORM\Entity]: the class is an entity; #[ORM\Table]: its table
#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'personnes')]
class Personne
{
     // the primary key, generated by the database (AUTO_INCREMENT); null before insertion
     #[ORM\Id]
     #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
     #[ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

     // the VERSION of the line: Doctrine increments it with each modification, and does not
     // modifies the row only if its version has not changed since it was read (optimistic lock
     // optimistic); the column type must be specified explicitly
     #[ORM\Version]
     #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    private int $version = 0;

     // the columns: their type SQL is derived from the type PHP (string: VARCHAR)
     #[ORM\Column(length: 30)]
    private string $prenom;

     #[ORM\Column(length: 30)]
    private string $nom;

     #[ORM\Column]
    private int $age;

    public function __construct(string $prenom, string $nom, int $age)
    {
        $this->modifier($prenom, $nom, $age);
    }

    public function modifier(string $prenom, string $nom, int $age): void
    {
        $this->prenom = $prenom;
        $this->nom = $nom;
        $this->age = $age;
    }

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getVersion(): int
    {
        return $this->version;
    }

    public function getPrenom(): string
    {
        return $this->prenom;
    }

    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return $this->nom;
    }

    public function getAge(): int
    {
        return $this->age;
    }
}
  • lines 10–11: the attribute [#[ORM\Entity]] designates the class as an entity; [#[ORM\Table]] specifies the name of its table (otherwise, [Doctrine] would take the name of the class, [personne]). [ORM] is an alias for the namespace [Doctrine\ORM\Mapping] (line 7): [use ... as ORM] allows attributes to be written in a shorthand form;
  • Lines 15–18: The primary key ([#[ORM\Id]]), generated by the database ([#[ORM\GeneratedValue]]: derived from [AUTO_INCREMENT], which is derived from [MySQL]). It is [null] until the entity has been inserted;
  • lines 23–25: the row version. The [#[ORM\Version]] attribute grants [Doctrine] the optimistic lock, described below;
  • lines 28–35: the columns. Each property marked [#[ORM\Column]] corresponds to the column of the same name; its type, SQL, is derived from the type [PHP] ([string]: [VARCHAR], of length [length]; [int]: [INT]). Unlike [Eloquent], the columns are declared: the class specifies exactly what the table contains;
  • lines 37–72: the entity is an ordinary class: a constructor, a method that modifies the person, and accessors. The properties are private: a person can only be modified through its methods. [Doctrine], on the other hand, reads and writes the properties directly (via reflection), without going through the constructor or the methods.

In a standard project, the [bin/console make:entity] command from [MakerBundle] writes the entity, asking a few questions about its properties.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Dao/PersonnesDao.php: the DAO layer, requests, no business rules

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Personne;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class PersonnesDao
{
     // the GESTIONNAIRE from Doctrine’s ENTITÉS: it reads and writes entities
    public function __construct(private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

     // SELECT ... FROM people ORDER BY last name, first name
     /** @return list<Person> */
    public function lister(): array
    {
        return $this->em->getRepository(Personne::class)->findBy([], ['nom' => 'ASC', 'prenom' => 'ASC']);
    }

     // SELECT ... FROM people WHERE id = ? ; null if the person does not exist
    public function lire(int $id): ?Personne
    {
        return $this->em->find(Personne::class, $id);
    }

     // a person with the same first and last name, other than [$saufId], written as DQL, the
     // Doctrine's query language: it refers to entities and properties, not
     // tables and columns
    public function homonyme(string $prenom, string $nom, int $saufId = 0): ?Personne
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT p FROM App\Entity\Personne p WHERE p.prenom = :prenom AND p.nom = :nom AND p.id <> :id')
            ->setParameters(['prenom' => $prenom, 'nom' => $nom, 'id' => $saufId])
            ->setMaxResults(1)
            ->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

     // INSERT (new entity) or UPDATE (entity read, then modified): `persist` hands
     // the entity to the manager; flush sends the necessary commands SQL to the database
    public function enregistrer(Personne $personne): void
    {
        $this->em->persist($personne);
        $this->em->flush();
    }

     // DELETE FROM people WHERE id = ?
    public function supprimer(Personne $personne): void
    {
        $this->em->remove($personne);
        $this->em->flush();
    }
}

The DAO layer contains only queries, with no business logic. It receives the entity manager (line 12), which uses the connection from the current query and participates in the open transaction—if there is one—initiated by the business layer.

  • Lines 18–21: Each entity has a repository (repository), an object that retrieves it from the database: [getRepository]. Its method [findBy(critères, tri)] returns the list of entities that match the criteria (in this case, none: all of them), in the requested order. (A repository also has [findAll], [findOneBy], [count].... ; an application can write its own repository class, with its own queries: this is what [make:entity] generates.) ;
  • lines 24–27: [find]: retrieval by primary key, or [null];
  • lines 32–39: a query written in DQL (Doctrine Query Language), the query language of [Doctrine]. It resembles SQL, but refers to entities and properties ([App\Entity\Personne p], [p.prenom]), which [Doctrine] translates into tables and columns. The values are named parameters ([:prenom]), provided by [setParameters]: they are transmitted to the database separately and are never copied into the text of the SQL command, which makes SQL injection impossible. [setMaxResults(1)] limits the result to one line ([LIMIT 1]); [getOneOrNullResult] returns the found entity, or [null];
  • Lines 43–47: The record. [persist] assigns a new entity to the manager (an entity read by the manager has already been assigned to him); [flush] sends all necessary SQL commands to the database: a [INSERT] for a new entity, and a [UPDATE] containing only the modified columns for an entity that was read and then modified. The manager compares each entity it has read to its original state: this is change tracking. After a [INSERT], [Doctrine] stores the ID generated by the database in the entity;
  • lines 50–54: the deletion: [remove], followed by [flush], which triggers [DELETE].

docs.title: 9.1.5. The business layer
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Metier/DonneesPersonne.php: a person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer

namespace App\Metier;

readonly class DonneesPersonne
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $prenom,
        public string $nom,
        public int $age,
    ) {
    }
}

A person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer: a simple object, unrelated to [Symfony].

<?php
// src/Metier/MetierException.php: a business rule rejects the operation; the
// This message is intended for the user

namespace App\Metier;

use RuntimeException;

class MetierException extends RuntimeException
{
}

An exception class specific to the business layer: a business rule rejects the operation, and the exception message is intended for the user. It inherits from [RuntimeException] without adding anything to it—only its name matters.

<?php
// src/Metier/PersonnesMetier.php: the MÉTIER layer, the business rules, and they
// alone. Every operation that writes is a TRANSACTION: validated (COMMIT) if the
// function completes normally, or rolled back (ROLLBACK) if an exception is thrown

namespace App\Metier;

use App\Dao\PersonnesDao;
use App\Entity\Personne;
use Doctrine\DBAL\Exception\UniqueConstraintViolationException;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;
use Doctrine\ORM\OptimisticLockException;

class PersonnesMetier
{
    private const HOMONYME = 'Une personne porte déjà ces prénom et nom.';

    private const MODIFIEE = 'Cette fiche a été modifiée entre-temps : rechargez-la.';

    private const INCONNUE = "Cette personne n'existe pas (ou plus).";

    public function __construct(private PersonnesDao $dao, private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

     /** @return list<Person> */
    public function lister(): array
    {
        return $this->dao->lister();
    }

    public function lire(int $id): Personne
    {
        return $this->dao->lire($id) ?? throw new MetierException(self::INCONNUE);
    }

    public function ajouter(DonneesPersonne $donnees): Personne
    {
         // wrapInTransaction: The function is executed within a transaction
        return $this->transaction(function () use ($donnees) {
             // Rule 1: No two people can have the same first and last names
            if ($this->dao->homonyme($donnees->prenom, $donnees->nom)) {
                throw new MetierException(self::HOMONYME);
            }
            $personne = new Personne($donnees->prenom, $donnees->nom, $donnees->age);
            $this->dao->enregistrer($personne);
            return $personne;
        });
    }

    public function modifier(int $id, int $version, DonneesPersonne $donnees): Personne
    {
        return $this->transaction(function () use ($id, $version, $donnees) {
            $personne = $this->lire($id);
             // Rule 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else
            if ($personne->getVersion() !== $version) {
                throw new MetierException(self::MODIFIEE);
            }
            if ($this->dao->homonyme($donnees->prenom, $donnees->nom, $id)) {
                throw new MetierException(self::HOMONYME);
            }
            $personne->modifier($donnees->prenom, $donnees->nom, $donnees->age);
             // Doctrine’s UPDATE “WHERE id = ... AND version = ...” raises an
             // OptimisticLockException if it has not modified any rows (see transaction)
            $this->dao->enregistrer($personne);
            return $personne;
        });
    }

    public function supprimer(int $id): Personne
    {
        return $this->transaction(function () use ($id) {
            $personne = $this->lire($id);
            $this->dao->supprimer($personne);
            return $personne;
        });
    }

     // the function [$operation], executed within a transaction. Two database errors
     // database are business errors: the uniqueness constraint (two simultaneous inserts),
     // and the optimistic lock (two simultaneous updates)
    private function transaction(callable $operation): Personne
    {
        try {
            return $this->em->wrapInTransaction($operation);
        } catch (UniqueConstraintViolationException $e) {
            throw new MetierException(self::HOMONYME, previous: $e);
        } catch (OptimisticLockException $e) {
            throw new MetierException(self::MODIFIEE, previous: $e);
        }
    }
}
  • lines 16–20: the business rule messages;
  • lines 32–35: a nonexistent person is a business error. The operator [??] accepts an expression [throw] on the right-hand side: if the person is [null], the exception is thrown;
  • lines 37–49: Rule No. 1: No two people may have the same first and last names. The rule is checked before writing to the database, and a [MetierException] exception is thrown if it is not satisfied. But this check is not sufficient: two simultaneous requests could both verify that there are no namesakes, and then both proceed to insert the records. The database’s uniqueness constraint then rejects the second [INSERT], and [Doctrine] triggers a [UniqueConstraintViolationException], which the [transaction] method transforms into the same [MetierException]. The database is the last line of defense;
  • lines 51–68: Rule No. 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else. The update form carries the version of the record that was read (in a hidden field); if it differs from the current version, the record has changed since it was displayed. There remains the case where the concurrent modification occurs between the read in line 54 and the save in line 65: this is detected by the optimistic lock in [Doctrine]. For an entity that has a version, [UPDATE] checks two conditions—the ID and the read version—and increments the version by 1; if another query has modified the row in the meantime—its version has changed—the [UPDATE] lock does not modify any rows, and [Doctrine] releases a [OptimisticLockException] lock. This is the principle of optimistic locking: nothing is blocked, but concurrent modifications are detected. ([Doctrine] does this itself, as do [Hibernate] and [SQLAlchemy]; the [Laravel] version of this course had to write the condition by hand.);
  • lines 70–77: Deletion marks the person as deleted for the confirmation message;
  • Lines 82–91: Every operation that writes data is executed within a transaction: [wrapInTransaction] opens the transaction, executes the function, submits the pending changes ([flush]), then commits the transaction ([COMMIT]) and returns the function’s value; If an exception is thrown from the function, the transaction is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): none of the changes made within the function are retained, and the exception is propagated. The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation, one transaction. The two database errors that are business errors become [MetierException]; the parameter named [previous] attaches the original exception to the new one for the log. Another error is returned as-is: it is not a business error, but a programming error (or a system failure). After an exception, [Doctrine] closes the entity manager, whose state is no longer reliable: it can no longer be used during the query, which is not a problem here, since the query is ending.

The parameter [callable] of the method [transaction] refers to an arbitrary function; the anonymous functions on lines 40, 53, and 72 capture, via [use], the variables they need.

docs.title: 9.1.6. The Web Layer
docs.text:
Form input is described by a class, and its constraints by attributes (Example 19):

<?php
// src/Form/PersonneSaisie.php: the form fields and their constraints (see Example 19)

namespace App\Form;

use App\Entity\Personne;
use App\Metier\DonneesPersonne;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints as Assert;

class PersonneSaisie
{
     #[Assert\NotBlank(message: 'Le prénom est obligatoire.')]
     #[Assert\Length(max: 30, maxMessage: '30 caractères au plus.')]
    public ?string $prenom = null;

     #[Assert\NotBlank(message: 'Le nom est obligatoire.')]
     #[Assert\Length(max: 30, maxMessage: '30 caractères au plus.')]
    public ?string $nom = null;

     #[Assert\NotNull(message: "L'âge est obligatoire.")]
     #[Assert\Range(notInRangeMessage: "L'âge doit être compris entre 0 et 150.", min: 0, max: 150)]
    public ?int $age = null;

     // the record version, carried by a hidden field (update only)
    public ?int $version = null;

     // the entry, pre-filled with an existing person
    public static function depuis(Personne $p): self
    {
        $saisie = new self();
        $saisie->prenom = $p->getPrenom();
        $saisie->nom = $p->getNom();
        $saisie->age = $p->getAge();
        $saisie->version = $p->getVersion();
        return $saisie;
    }

     // the validated data for the business layer
    public function donnees(): DonneesPersonne
    {
        return new DonneesPersonne(trim($this->prenom), trim($this->nom), $this->age);
    }
}
  • lines 12–22: the constraints, with messages in French;
  • line 25: the record version, carried by a hidden field (edit mode only);
  • lines 28–36: a pre-filled entry with an existing person, for the update form;
  • lines 39–42: the validated data, in the format expected by the business layer.

We could have linked the form directly to the [Personne] entity (option [data_class], Example 19) and placed the constraints on it: this is common with [Symfony]. However, the form would then modify the entity before the business layer had verified its rules, and an invalid entity would be passed to the entity manager. A separate input class keeps the layers distinct: the web layer transmits only validated data to the business layer.

<?php
// src/Form/PersonneType.php: a person’s form (see Example 18)

namespace App\Form;

use Symfony\Component\Form\AbstractType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\HiddenType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\IntegerType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\TextType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\FormBuilderInterface;
use Symfony\Component\OptionsResolver\OptionsResolver;

class PersonneType extends AbstractType
{
    public function buildForm(FormBuilderInterface $builder, array $options): void
    {
        $builder
            ->add('prenom', TextType::class, ['label' => 'Prénom', 'attr' => ['maxlength' => 30]])
            ->add('nom', TextType::class, ['label' => 'Nom', 'attr' => ['maxlength' => 30]])
            ->add('age', IntegerType::class, ['label' => 'Âge', 'attr' => ['min' => 0, 'max' => 150],
                'invalid_message' => "L'âge doit être un nombre entier."]);
         // the version: a hidden field, in the edit form only
        if ($options['modification']) {
            $builder->add('version', HiddenType::class);
        }
    }

     // form options: the data class, and a custom option
    public function configureOptions(OptionsResolver $resolver): void
    {
        $resolver->setDefaults(['data_class' => PersonneSaisie::class, 'modification' => false]);
    }
}
  • lines 20–21: an integer field; [invalid_message] is the message displayed when the input cannot be converted to an integer;
  • lines 23–25: the hidden version field, in the update form only, according to the option [modification];
  • lines 29–32: [configureOptions] declares the form options and their default values: the data class, and a custom option, [modification].
<?php
// src/Controller/PersonnesController.php: the WEB layer; it only knows the business layer

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Form\PersonneSaisie;
use App\Form\PersonneType;
use App\Metier\MetierException;
use App\Metier\PersonnesMetier;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\Form\FormInterface;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\AccessDeniedHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

// name: a prefix for the names of all routes in the class (personnes_liste...)
#[Route(name: 'personnes_')]
class PersonnesController extends AbstractController
{
    public function __construct(private PersonnesMetier $metier)
    {
    }

     #[Route('/', name: 'accueil', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function accueil(): Response
    {
        return $this->redirectToRoute('personnes_liste');
    }

     #[Route('/personnes', name: 'liste', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function liste(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('personnes/liste.html.twig', ['personnes' => $this->metier->lister()]);
    }

     // GET: the empty form; POST: the submitted form
     #[Route('/personnes/ajout', name: 'ajout', methods: ['GET', 'POST'])]
    public function ajout(Request $request): Response
    {
        $saisie = new PersonneSaisie();
        $formulaire = $this->createForm(PersonneType::class, $saisie);
        $formulaire->handleRequest($request);
        if ($formulaire->isSubmitted() && $formulaire->isValid()) {
            try {
                $p = $this->metier->ajouter($saisie->donnees());
                $this->addFlash('succes', "{$p->getPrenom()} {$p->getNom()} a été ajouté(e).");
                return $this->redirectToRoute('personnes_liste');
            } catch (MetierException $e) {
                 // A business rule rejects the form: the form is redisplayed, with the
                 // data entered, and the message at the bottom of the page
                return $this->pageFormulaire('Ajouter une personne', $formulaire, $e->getMessage());
            }
        }
        return $this->pageFormulaire('Ajouter une personne', $formulaire);
    }

     // GET: the edit form, pre-filled
     #[Route('/personnes/{id<\d+>}/modification', name: 'modification', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function modification(int $id): Response
    {
        try {
            $p = $this->metier->lire($id);
        } catch (MetierException $e) {
            $this->addFlash('erreur', $e->getMessage());
            return $this->redirectToRoute('personnes_liste');
        }
        return $this->pageFormulaire('Modifier une personne', $this->formulaireModification($id, PersonneSaisie::depuis($p)));
    }

     // PUT: the modification form has been submitted
     #[Route('/personnes/{id<\d+>}', name: 'modifier', methods: ['PUT'])]
    public function modifier(Request $request, int $id): Response
    {
        $saisie = new PersonneSaisie();
        $formulaire = $this->formulaireModification($id, $saisie);
        $formulaire->handleRequest($request);
        if ($formulaire->isSubmitted() && $formulaire->isValid()) {
            try {
                $p = $this->metier->modifier($id, (int) $saisie->version, $saisie->donnees());
                $this->addFlash('succes', "{$p->getPrenom()} {$p->getNom()} a été modifié(e).");
                return $this->redirectToRoute('personnes_liste');
            } catch (MetierException $e) {
                return $this->pageFormulaire('Modifier une personne', $formulaire, $e->getMessage());
            }
        }
        return $this->pageFormulaire('Modifier une personne', $formulaire);
    }

     #[Route('/personnes/{id<\d+>}', name: 'supprimer', methods: ['DELETE'])]
    public function supprimer(Request $request, int $id): Response
    {
        if (! $this->isCsrfTokenValid("supprimer-personne-$id", $request->request->getString('_token'))) {
            throw new AccessDeniedHttpException('jeton anti-CSRF invalide');
        }
        try {
            $p = $this->metier->supprimer($id);
            $this->addFlash('succes', "{$p->getPrenom()} {$p->getNom()} a été supprimé(e).");
        } catch (MetierException $e) {
             // No form to redisplay: the error is also conveyed via a flash message
            $this->addFlash('erreur', $e->getMessage());
        }
        return $this->redirectToRoute('personnes_liste');
    }

     // the update form: sent via the PUT method to URL /people/{id}
    private function formulaireModification(int $id, PersonneSaisie $saisie): FormInterface
    {
        return $this->createForm(PersonneType::class, $saisie, ['modification' => true,
            'method' => 'PUT', 'action' => $this->generateUrl('personnes_modifier', ['id' => $id])]);
    }

    private function pageFormulaire(string $titre, FormInterface $formulaire, ?string $erreur = null): Response
    {
         // A business error: code 422, as for an invalid form (see example 19)
        return $this->render('personnes/formulaire.html.twig',
            ['titre' => $titre, 'formulaire' => $formulaire, 'erreur' => $erreur],
            new Response(status: $erreur ? 422 : 200));
    }
}
  • line 18: The class attribute [#[Route]] prefixes only the route names here: the route named [liste] is actually called [personnes_liste];
  • line 21: the business layer, the only layer known to the controller;
  • lines 38–56: the process, in three steps: form validation (input errors, Example 19); the call to the business layer (business rules); then the PRG schema, with a success flash message (Example 20). A [MetierException] re-displays the form, along with the entered data and the exception message, which the template will display at the bottom of the page. Input errors and business logic errors are thus handled in the same way;
  • lines 59–69: the edit form, pre-filled with the retrieved person. If the person does not exist, the user is redirected to the list with a flash error message;
  • lines 72–88: the update, following the same pattern as the add operation;
  • lines 90–104: deletion, protected by a CSRF token unique to each person (example 21). There is no form to redisplay: any error is also conveyed in a flash message, [erreur];
  • lines 107–111: the edit form is submitted using the method PUT (option [method]: [form_start] then adds the hidden field [_method], Example 21), to URL [/personnes/{id}] (option [action]);
  • lines 113–119: the form page. A business error is returned with code 422, indicating an invalid form.

The web layer contains neither SQL nor any business rules: it translates the request into a call to the business layer and the result into a page.

The views:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Personnes</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ path('bootstrap', {fichier: 'css/bootstrap.min.css'}) }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ asset('css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {# the success message (flash message [succes]): at the top #}
    {% for message in app.flashes('succes') %}
      <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
    <main>
      {% block contenu %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    {# errors: at the bottom; a flash message [erreur], or the variable [erreur] from the view #}
    {% for message in app.flashes('erreur') %}
      <div class="zone-erreur" role="alert">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
    {% if erreur is defined and erreur %}
      <div class="zone-erreur" role="alert">{{ erreur }}</div>
    {% endif %}
  </div>
  {% include 'fragments/confirmation.html.twig' %}
  <script src="{{ asset('js/app.js') }}"></script>
</body>
</html>
  • lines 13–15: the success message at the top of the page (example 20);
  • Lines 20–25: errors; at the bottom of the page: a flash message (after a redirect), or the view variable [erreur] (form re-displayed). The test [is defined] prevents an error on pages that do not have this variable.
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">Personnes</h1>
  <table class="table align-middle">
    <thead><tr><th>Prénom</th><th>Nom</th><th>Âge</th><th></th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for p in personnes %}
        <tr>

          <td class="text-end">

              <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger" type="submit">Supprimer</button>

  <a class="btn btn-primary" href="{{ path('personnes_ajout') }}">Ajouter une personne</a>

The list includes the links and buttons from Example 21, along with its confirmation window (the files [fragments/confirmation.html.twig] and [public/js/app.js] are those from Example 21). The properties [p.prenom], [p.nom]... are read by the accessors [getPrenom()], [getNom()]... : [Twig] finds them on its own (Example 13).

{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">{{ titre }}</h1>
  {# novalidate: validation is performed by the server (see example 19); form_start
     écrit aussi le champ caché _method d'un formulaire PUT #}
  {{ form_start(formulaire, {attr: {novalidate: 'novalidate'}}) }}
    {{ form_widget(formulaire) }}

A view used for both adding and modifying records. [form_widget] renders all form fields, including the hidden version field and the anti-CSRF token.
